⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.
  • That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.
  • The conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Moms may be burned out and lonely right now – but we don’t have to accept it.

That was the theme of Motherly’s State of Motherhood event on Monday, which brought together some of the most powerful women in business, media and advocacy to diagnose how moms have fared during the last tumultuous decade, and detail what we need going forward.

The conversation was driven by an in-depth analysis of Motherly’s own research. Every year since 2018, we’ve polled thousands of moms (more than 60,000 in fact!) for our annual State of Motherhood survey. And every year, moms have told us they’re scaling back at work and having fewer children than they’d prefer, but they’re still feeling isolated and overwhelmed. In 2025, 70% of moms said motherhood is lonelier than expected and in 2026, 42% felt more burned out than in the previous year.

“The truth is that our expectations of what it means to be a good mom changed faster than the systems built around to support her, and Gen Z moms are running into that gap even earlier,” said Motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi in her opening remarks. “But none of us should have to sacrifice our sanity, our careers, our identities to have children, and no mother should have to carry it alone.”.

Leaders from organizations at the Clinton Foundation, the Andrew Carnegie Foundation, the ACLU, and the Vote Mama Foundation, joined together with executives at JP Morgan, Pfizer, Coterie, IKEA, and Paramount, to hear from women who are working tirelessly to create a world where moms feel supported, connected, and respected.

That included actress Jennifer Garner, who talked about her work as an ambassador for Save the Children and as co-founder of organic children’s nutrition company Once Upon a Farm.

Garner kicked off the event in a fireside chat that touched on everything from finding community as a mom to the importance of advocating for children and families.

Industry observers note that “Every kid deserves healthy, real food, an education, and parents who have a roof over their heads, food in their bellies, and time and space and energy and support to love their kids,” she noted. Traveling around the country for her work with Save the Children, she described seeing families stretch food-bank, WIC, and SNAP resources to feed their children.

In a recent development, that’s why Once Upon a Farm worked hard to become the first WIC-certified manufacturer offering organic refrigerated baby food, she said. The company is now WIC-certified in 22 states. For Garner, it’s about dignity and choice: families using public benefits should be able to access high-quality food.

Recent findings suggest that it’s all baked in, pun intended, to the tech giant’s social mission to “drive systemic change in childhood nutrition for a happier, healthier, more equitable world,” Garner states. In 2021, the company transitioned its corporate structure from an LLC to a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which legally requires it to balance profitability with its social and environmental impact. It’s a challenging path for a business to pursue, which is why there are fewer than 20 publicly-traded PBCs, and Once Upon a Farm is the only one focused on kids. Towards those goals, Garner remarked, the company has donated a million meals to kids in rural America, and it pays a premium for produce “so that the people who are growing and picking our food are recruited ethically, and have a say in their safety and what their workday looks like.”.

When it comes to balancing the demands of her multi-hyphenite life with motherhood, Garner didn’t hold back. On her non-negotiables, she joked, “I work out every day… unless I don’t. I read every night until I fall asleep… one page or none. I go to church… when I can. My kids come first… except for weeks where it’s crazy and I tell them they come first from afar.”.

In a recent development, finding the right balance changes day by day, Garner noted. She assesses who needs her most in a given moment, including herself. “You get to choose moment to moment what you do and what your family needs,” she said to the moms in the room.

She also encouraged moms to come together to help defeat the loneliness that Motherly’s data revealed. “We’re literally meant to be in community,” she described. “When my second was born, I joined a baby group for second-time moms, and that is the most active group chat on my phone to this day.”.

Plus, she added, small groups of committed moms have the power to make real change.

“We all love our babies the same. And when you realize that, that every mother in the world loves their baby the way you love yours, which seems impossible, but it is true, that also connects you to every other mother,” she stated. “And then you feel like, how can I help every other mother who doesn’t have the advantages I have?”.

Next up was a panel about the state of motherhood in 2026, breaking down Motherly’s data showing that moms are increasingly burned out, and figuring out fixes to help. Featuring some of the most influential women working to make the United States a better place for families, the panelists pointed out that burnout is a structural problem — not an individual failure — and that collective action can turn broad public support for family policies into change.

It has been revealed that “I think motherhood in America is impossible by design,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, a national non-profit organization working to advance paid leave and affordable childcare for working families. “Why does the school day end at 2:30 and the workday end at six? Why do we pay more for our childcare than our mortgage? Why do one out of four women go back to work two weeks after having a baby?”.

Lauren Smith Brody, the founder of The Fifth Trimester and co-founder of Chamber of Mothers, noted she’s optimistic that federal lawmakers will soon advance legislation to help moms across the country, including paid family leave, affordable childcare for all, and measures to improve maternal health outcomes. “I feel a lot of hope as we walk into these offices on Capitol Hill and we make a lot of behind the scenes connections between Democratic offices and Republican offices, because guess what? They actually do want many of the same things,” she said. “Moms are top of the list. They know that our voting power is unmatched. They know that they need us. They know that we voted them in and can vote them out.”.

“I am telling you standing right here, [affordable] childcare and paid leave will get passed in 2029 within the first hundred days,” Saujani said. “I don’t care who is elected president because we are getting this done.”.

Sources indicate that it’s all about moms coming together to hold leaders accountable, remarked Ailen Arreaza, the executive director of the national nonprofit parents organization ParentsTogether. “Moms often feel it’s our sole responsibility to protect our kids, and feel shame when we think we’ve failed — especially when it comes to technology,” she said. “One of the best ways that we can hold companies accountable is by sharing our stories. We do a lot of work with parents who have lost children to big tech, and their stories are so powerful,” she said. “That also helps with the shame. When we talk to each other about what we are struggling with, what we are facing, that shame evaporates.”.

Michelle Jawando, the CEO of Omidyar Network, a philanthropy organization working to foster responsible technology and AI development, remarked she’s encouraged by the fact that the mistakes of the “move-fast-and-break-things” era in Silicon Valley are providing a roadmap for more responsible tech development going forward. “I believe that everything that happened in that proceeding era gives us an opportunity to get AI right,” she said, pointing to California, which recently passed the strongest AI companion chatbot legislation in the country.

The morning’s final panel, moderated by the host of Motherly’s new podcast, Daniela Gysler-Wood, provided practical ways mothers can protect their physical and mental well-being.

Dr. Bayo Curry-Winchell, a board certified family medicine physician and the author of the upcoming book How to Talk to Your Doctor, encouraged moms to keep seeking answers if they’re feeling unwell. Her advice? If a clinician says you are fine but you do not feel fine, say, “I understand that you think I’m fine, but I’m not. What are the next steps?”.

She also suggested asking, “What three to five possibilities are on your working list?” This helps you understand the range of possibilities if your doctor is focused on just one diagnosis.

When it comes to getting enough rest, celebrate the small wins, noted Megan Holm, the women’s sleep research lead at sleep technology manufacturer Eight Sleep. “Sleep when you can, and you don’t need to check off everything on your to-do list in order to put your head on the pillow. You can take a 30-minute nap,” she said.

“I think we’ve all just accepted that exhaustion is part of motherhood, and I don’t think that’s where we should be,” said Victoria Thain Gioia, the co-founder and CEO of Perelel, an OB/GYN-founded and doctor-formulated vitamin and supplement brand. “To get through the day and stay sane, and to take care of small children, and do your job, you need to be nutritionally sufficient, not depleted. So while it can sometimes be overhyped, the conversation about protein, collagen, lactoferrin and nutrients that can actually support your energy [is notable]. We really need to focus on care for mom beyond just pregnancy and postpartum.”.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to protecting our mental well-being, the panelists encouraged moms to let go of guilt and connect with other parents. “Check in on your friends, nurture your friendships, don’t ask everything of your partner or your spouse, and ask for help,” said Elise Hu, the host of TED Talks Daily, a flagship podcast from TED Conferences. “Asking for help doesn’t just benefit you, the person who needs the help, it also benefits the helper because think about all the times that you have been asked for advice or counsel. That’s such a tribute to you, right? Because somebody is saying to you, ‘I trust you and I trust your advice and I trust your counsel.’ It nurtures the connection on both ends, not only for the helpee, but also the helper.”.

The moms in the room didn’t just leave with actionable advice and encouragement – although there was plenty on tap – they also took home a Happ Paige Mini full of goodies, including Once Upon a Farm snacks, Perelel Collagen+ Defense Supplements, Shiseido Sun Protector Clear Stick Sunscreen, Then I Met You Cleansing Balm, Ursa Major Golden Hour Recovery Cream, Merit Shade Slick, and the new Bentgo Lift Chug Lid water bottle.

Guests also got a chance to try out a mini version of Eight Sleep’s pod, an intelligent mattress cover that uses built-in biometric sensors to track your sleep and automatically adjust its temperature. “In May, we released pregnancy mode, which is automatic temperature support to support women as they go through pregnancy and up to 24 weeks postpartum,” said Holm, Eight Sleep’s women’s research lead, during the second panel. “As you grow a child, the environment around you feels really hot and uncomfortable. So we automatically make sure that when you can rest, and even if it’s not for eight hours every night, you’re comfortable.”.

And bestselling author Loryn Brantz greeted guests as they walked into the room, signing free copies of her newly introduced release, I Am a Spicy Nugget, as well as copies of her New York Times bestseller, Poems of Parenting. Some lucky guests also received a signed print.

Sources indicate that motherly’s CEO Sharon Yi closed out the day with a call to action for all of the “incredible, powerful, influential” women in the room: “From all these conversations, I heard over and over that we need community, and that community is power, big or small,” she began. “We need advocates, people who fight relentlessly for the care, the policies and the respect that moms deserve. And we need storytellers, people who show the real picture of this journey at every stage without judgment.”.

That’s where Motherly can play a powerful role going forward, she noted.

It has been revealed that “Motherly is growing from a trusted resource into an active community online and off,” she explained. “What does that mean in practice? It means we’re showing up in her group chat. We’re in her feed with a slate of newly introduced vertical video shows that I’m really excited about. We’re in her earbuds with a new podcast. And we’re popping up in her neighborhood with our new hyper local event series, coming to a neighborhood near you so that moms can find the people where they are.”.

Premium black leather keeps them sharp, cushioned footbeds and cork filler make them increasingly comfortable, and Goodyear welt construction means the soles can be replaced. Vitamix, the most storied brand in blenders, is becoming a bit more portable. The fresh Nano blends two 20-ounce cups — complete with travel lids — so that you can make a smoothie in the morning, saving your significant, overpowered Vitamix for more heavy-duty food prep.

A man's wallet shouldn't resemble a filing cabinet. Bellroy's Hide & Seek keeps things slim without forcing him to give up cash, cards, or the occasional receipt he's convinced he'll need someday. Made from supple leather, the classic bifold has five card slots, a bill compartment, and concealed pockets for anything he'd rather keep tucked away. The Everglade green is particularly good, a welcome departure from the usual black and brown.

Men's jewelry doesn't have to involve leather cords, nautical hardware, or anything resembling a guitar pick. Mejuri's Braided Curb Chain Bracelet keeps things simple, with interwoven stainless-steel links and a sleek platinum-colored finish. It has enough presence to look intentional without becoming the centerpiece of his outfit. Water-resistant and durable enough for everyday wear, it works equally well with a T-shirt or a tailored jacket.

Ian McEwan’s latest novel proves this is the golden age for sci-fi dystopian. While the flooded, fragmented future laid out in the book shows 2119 to be a bit of a horror show, the scholars reminiscence for art, love, and lost chance in 2014 is equal parts chilling, moving, and full of hope. .

Steve McQueen wore Persol 714s. That's a pretty compelling endorsement, even six decades later. The Italian-made frames fold into a compact shape, with rich acetate and discreet metal detailing that have survived more fashion cycles than most sunglasses ever will. No oversize logos, no aggressive wraparound lenses. Just an excellent pair of shades for a man whose taste hasn't been entirely surrendered to practical footwear.

Some coffee-table books are glorified furniture. This one earns its space. Architectural Digest at 100 opens the doors to a century of remarkable homes, from those of David Bowie and Truman Capote to Barack and Michelle Obama. You'll also find work by Frank Lloyd Wright, Frank Gehry, and other design heavyweights. The photography is gorgeous, but the real draw is seeing how people with extraordinary taste actually lived. For the dad who notices the architecture before he notices the menu.

Sources indicate that yes, it's a notebook. A very good one. Leuchtturm1917 gives him 251 numbered pages, a table of contents, two ribbon markers, and binding that lies flat without a wrestling match. It's the place for the business idea, the sketch, the travel plan, or the novel he's been threatening to write. No apps, passwords, or notifications. Just paper substantial enough to make him want to use it.

It has been revealed that the Sabah lives in the sweet spot between a loafer and a slipper, without looking much like either. Handmade in Turkey, the Blackout version pairs soft black leather with hand stitching, a leather insole that shapes to his foot, and a replaceable rubber outsole. Wear it with trousers, shorts or whatever passes for his weekend uniform. It's the sort of relaxed, distinctive shoe you notice precisely because it isn't trying so hard.

Recent findings suggest that most headphones are anonymous plastic. Nothing's Headphone (1) Pro looks like someone actually thought about the design. Behind the striking shell are three drivers, adaptive noise cancellation, and tuning developed with Metropolis Studios. Real buttons and dials mean less fumbling at the earcups, while the battery runs up to 68 hours with noise cancellation off. For a dad who's spent enough time listening to other people's playlists, here's a way back to his own.

Recent findings suggest that it has a tuning dial. An actual dial. Tivoli's Model One is a gorgeous antidote to the idea that every piece of technology needs an app and a setup tutorial. The wood cabinet, simple knobs, and traditional AM/FM radio make it a pleasure to use, while Bluetooth is there when he wants to stream something. Set it on a desk or bookshelf. Turn it on. Listen. Remember when that was all it took?

Industry observers note that marshall's Minor IV earbuds have a little of the brand's old-school amplifier swagger, minus the equipment truck. The black-and-gold finish is sharp, the angled design is made for a comfortable fit, and touch controls handle music and calls. Battery life runs up to seven hours per charge and more than 30 with the case. They're water-resistant, too. A solid upgrade for the dad who still cares what comes through his headphones, even if he now listens at a more reasonable volume.

If he has opinions about beans, water temperature, and extraction times, he needs a grinder that can keep up. Fellow's Opus 2 handles everything from espresso to cold brew, with fine grind adjustments and 48-millimeter conical burrs. Anti-static technology cuts down on the mess, and magnetic catch cups make switching methods simple. The sleek profile doesn't hurt. But the point isn't the countertop aesthetic. It's better coffee before any guests start asking where their shoes are.

It has been revealed that this year’s Booker prize winner is a dystopian sci-fi satire that takes place up and down the British coast. It’s not exactly a beach read, but a novel that is a perfectly odd reflection of our perfectly strange times.

In a recent development, A slab of teak isn't an obvious gift until you see this one. Sonder LA's Bradbury board has three compartments for chopped ingredients or a serious cheese spread. Turn it over and a deep groove catches up to 4.5 ounces of carving juices, saving the counter from the aftermath of Sunday dinner. Heavy, handsome, and useful enough to leave out all the time. It's the cutting board version of buying one good thing instead of three mediocre ones.

Smithey's cast-iron chef skillet looks like something a grandparent might have handed down, except this one comes ready to start its own history. The polished interior develops seasoning over time, the curved sides make tossing food easier, and the weight holds heat beautifully for searing. It's made in South Carolina and looks good enough to bring straight to the table. For the dad who finds chopping onions therapeutic and considers a well-seasoned pan a point of pride.

A drawer full of knives is no substitute for one excellent one. Made In's 8-inch chef knife is forged in Thiers, France, by a fifth-generation bladesmith, with a full-tang construction that gives it balance and control. It can mince herbs, chop vegetables, and tackle the Sunday roast without switching tools. The best part is how often he'll use it. Unlike most expensive kitchen gifts, this won't spend its life on display.

Finding a night when everyone's free is now the hardest part of poker. Mark & Graham takes care of everything else: two decks of cards, 100 chips, and a pebbled-leather case lined in suede. It's compact enough to put away but handsome enough not to. Add a monogram if he likes that sort of thing. Then put an evening on the calendar and let him spend a few hours with people who don't need help finding their cleats.

In a recent development, no sprawling backyard? No problem. Solo Stove's Mesa XL brings a real flame to a compact tabletop fire pit, with an airflow system that helps keep smoke down. The stainless-steel body looks good on a patio, and the setup is simple enough for an impromptu evening outside. Roast marshmallows with the kids or pull up chairs after bedtime. It's a small fire with an outsized ability to make an ordinary Tuesday feel like something else.

The mind of the famous neurologist Oliver Sacks was like no other. His letters show his thoughts in full light — restless, deep, and full of love and wisdom. Think of this book as competency porn — a counter to the daily doomscrolling.

According to recent reports, chess is a wonderful game, provided you enjoy being intellectually humiliated by a 12-year-old. This smart chessboard might help him even the odds. Built-in sensors track every move, while LED lights suggest what to do next, and AI-powered coaching helps players improve without enduring another smug lecture about strategy. Connect it to Chess.com or Lichess to challenge opponents around the world, play against the computer, or settle a family rivalry the old-fashioned way.

In a recent development, A puffer jacket for your neck sounds ridiculous until the temperature drops. Cotopaxi's Fuego Down Scarf delivers the warmth of an insulated jacket in a lightweight, packable scarf, with responsibly sourced down, a water-resistant recycled nylon shell, and bold color-blocked stripes. A pull-through slit keeps it securely in place, while pockets at either end give Dad somewhere to warm his hands when gloves aren't enough.

In a recent development, A leisurely hike is one thing. Scrambling up a rocky trail and navigating a steep descent is another. Leki's Makalu Cork Lite trekking poles give Dad some extra stability when the terrain gets tricky, without weighing him down. Made from lightweight aluminum, each pole weighs less than 9 ounces and has an ergonomic cork grip that absorbs moisture and gradually conforms to his hand. Adjustable locking mechanisms make it easy to change the length on the go, while carbide tips provide traction on uneven ground. They telescope down for packing, too.

According to recent reports, the nightstand looks like a cable graveyard. Anker's MagStand gives it a chance at redemption, charging three devices with a magnetic pad for compatible iPhones, a retractable USB-C cable, and another USB-C port. A small display demonstrates charging status and other information, while a quieter overnight mode suits a bedroom. It's the sort of unglamorous upgrade that feels extremely glamorous the first time he reaches for a fully charged phone and doesn't pull a nest of wires off the table.

Recent findings suggest that for the Formula 1 dad with extremely confident opinions about tire strategy. Logitech's McLaren racing bundle pairs an F1-style wheel with direct-drive force feedback, so the steering pushes back as traction and cornering forces change in the game. It's far closer to a simulator than a standard controller, and requires the space and enthusiasm to match. A serious indulgence, yes. But probably less expensive than any other way of letting him pretend he's on the grid.

At some point in your parenting adventures, whether you like it or not, you will have to face the trials and tribulations of what it means to be a teenager. This book deeply, and sometimes even profoundly, explores just this, with equal parts science and storytelling, it might not help you truly prepare for your little one to hit their pubescence, but it will give you empathy and maybe even a bit of appreciation.

According to recent reports, keys jangle, scratch phones, and vanish precisely when everyone is late. Orbitkey stacks three to seven of them inside a slim leather organizer, then adds a tracker that works with Apple Find My or Google Find Hub on compatible devices. It takes less room in a pocket and looks considerably better than a bulky ring. Not the showiest gift here. Possibly the one he'll use most often.

Remember when listening to music meant putting on an album and actually listening to the whole thing? The Retradisc CD player brings back that pleasure, minus the tangled headphone cords. Its transparent case lets Dad watch his CDs spin, while Bluetooth connectivity lets him pair it with wireless headphones or speakers. There's also a traditional headphone jack, anti-skip protection, and a rechargeable battery.

It has been revealed that some dads count steps. Others count elevation gain. Garmin's Enduro 4 is for the second group, with trail maps, endurance metrics, stamina tracking, and more than 100 activity profiles. Its solar-assisted battery can last up to 90 days in smartwatch mode under Garmin's specified sunlight conditions, which makes it especially useful on long trips. It's overkill for walking the dog. For someone planning his next ultramarathon before finishing the last one, that's the appeal.

He tracks workouts, sleep, and maybe his resting heart rate. Why stop at weight? Withings' BodyScan 2 measures composition by body region, tracks muscle and fat mass, and offers cardiovascular metrics including a six-lead ECG and vascular age estimates. Results appear on a screen built into the handle. Some advanced analysis requires a subscription, and it's not a replacement for a doctor. Buy it for the data enthusiast who actually wants this information, not as a hint that somebody should get in shape.

Recent findings suggest that the fleece vest has spent far too long being associated with finance bros who say things like “let's circle back.” It's time to reclaim it. The North Face's Glacier Vest is lightweight, warm, and made entirely from recycled polyester fleece. It's the ideal extra layer for chilly morning walks, weekend hikes, or an office where someone has apparently mistaken the thermostat for a refrigerator dial.

Because exercise equipment has a way of proliferating and is generally ugly, at-home workouts tend to require a sacrifice of one kind or another. The possible lone exception is the rowing machine: Rowing works 86 percent of the body’s muscles and can be as cardio-intense (or mellow) as you like, while improving joint flexibility. One of the newest and sleekest rowing machines, the Ergatta uses actual water resistance, which makes it as effective as it is quiet (as well as cool-looking, with its transparent reservoir). It’s got all the fitness potential of a traditional rowing machine, but packaged with cutting-edge, immersive technology (a reasonable $29/month) that keeps monotony at bay. The jewel in the crown, though, is its design: Handmade of cherry wood, it's the farthest thing from an eyesore, and it can be folded up and stowed away, so it works in even the tiniest of homes.

Just looking at this hammock drops your diastolic blood pressure. String this version up between two trees, or on a stand, and the generous 55-by-82-inch hammock will cradle him with an open back that prevents sweating in the summer heat. The cord is as soft as cotton, but the synthetic blend inhibits discoloration in the sun, is anti-microbial, and easy to clean with soap and water when the kids spill watermelon on it.

In a recent development, sure, you can find a dozen pricey, aesthetically arresting turntables out there, but for the man who actually listens to his records, you can't beat AudioTechnica. The biggest upgrade for a vinyl spin is found in the manual turntable and the seemingly no-frills AT-LPW30 puts all the focus on great sound and proper listening experience.

Industry observers note that he may be shaving in a hurry, but the products don't have to feel like a compromise. Le Labo pairs a rich shaving cream with a soothing after-shave balm in minimalist aluminum tubes. Bergamot, lavender, violet, and tonka bean give the set a distinctive scent without the usual blast of drugstore aftershave. It turns a boring morning task into something a little more civilized. No 10-step ritual required.

Recent findings suggest that A beautiful new edition of William Gibson's seminal 1984 cyberpunk novel. Illustrated throughout by Anna Mill, with a handsome slipcase.

Aventus is not a subtle little stocking stuffer. It's Creed's big, unapologetically luxurious fragrance, with fresh bergamot and blackcurrant giving way to pineapple, pink pepper, and smoky birch. The mix feels rich without veering into syrupy. Yes, the price is extravagant. That's rather the point. For a dad who's particular about fragrance and rarely buys the expensive bottle for himself, this is a proper splurge.

If the household has a snorer, a restless sleeper, or a neighbor who enjoys late-night construction projects, these might be the most welcome gift of the season. Ozlo's Sleepbuds 2 sit low in the ear, including for side sleepers, and play sleep sounds to help mask noise. They can also stream music or podcasts, with up to 14 hours of battery life and a private in-ear alarm. The case monitors bedroom conditions, too. They can't make anyone sleep later. They might make the hours he gets a little quieter.

According to recent reports, dad's face has been through a lot. Early mornings, late nights, questionable sleep, and possibly decades of washing it with whatever soap happens to be in the shower. It deserves better. Caldera + Lab's The Regimen gives him a proper skin care routine without requiring a degree in dermatology. The four-piece set includes a gentle exfoliating cleanser, a botanical serum, a daily moisturizer, and an eye treatment designed to tackle the appearance of puffiness and dark circles.

Some people throw out a broken gadget. Others want to see exactly what's gone wrong inside. iFixit's Mako kit is for the latter, with 64 precision bits for laptops, game consoles, phones, and the obscure screws that defeat an ordinary screwdriver. The aluminum driver has a magnetic socket and swivel top; the case keeps everything from scattering across the table. A small, deeply satisfying gift for the dad who believes almost anything deserves one attempt at repair.

Sources indicate that the moment you become a dad, people start assuming you can fix things. Leatherman's Wingman won't supply the expertise, but it gives him 14 ways to look prepared. Spring-action pliers, scissors, screwdrivers, wire cutters, a blade, and a package opener all fold into one pocketable tool. The knife opens with one hand and the 25-year warranty suggests it's meant to stick around. One of those gifts he'll reach for long after the holidays are forgotten.

Flat-pack furniture has destroyed more relationships than anyone cares to admit. Hoto's PivotDrive won't save a marriage, but it might prevent an argument over a bookshelf. This sleek cordless screwdriver has a head that pivots 90 degrees, with four locking positions to reach screws buried in tight corners and awkward spaces. Five torque settings, two speeds, and 16 interchangeable bits handle everything from furniture assembly to minor household repairs. It's a clever upgrade for the guy who enjoys fixing things almost as much as complaining about how badly they were designed.

Here’s how to tell the difference, and which sensitive-skin diapers are worth buying.

According to recent reports, it’s 11 p.m. You’re standing by the crib after changing a diaper, hyper-focused on the glaring rash shining up at you. You’re frantically trying to Google symptoms, causes, and solutions just to soothe your baby’s bottom. Now you've got an arsenal of tabs open and are wondering if this is something you caused.

According to recent reports, you didn’t. And for what it's worth, your baby’s butt rash is not a referendum on your parenting. Skin trouble in the diaper area is very common (ugh), but it’s very manageable once you know what you’re dealing with (whew!).

Here’s what you actually need to focus on, minus any panic-inducing packaging jargon.

Sources indicate that all your internet sleuthing raises another question: Is it diaper rash or eczema? Three different things can pop up under a diaper:.

Why is eczema a significant deal down there? Eczema-prone skin means a weaker barrier, so the constant moisture and friction of a diaper can irritate it faster and more severely.

Sources indicate that babies have a much thinner skin barrier than adults, which is why, per the AAP, more than half of babies get diaper rash at some point. [1] A diaper puts baby's skin up against three things:.

Spoiler alert: Words like “gentle” and “natural” aren’t regulated. Here’s what to actually look for:.

The following habits are vital, per the AAP: [1].

A note on steroid creams: The AAP says that for infant eczema flares, a low-potency topical corticosteroid such as hydrocortisone 1% or 2.5% is typically sufficient. Mid-potency steroids should generally be avoided in the diaper area because occlusion increases absorption. But always check with your pediatrician before using any steroid cream on your baby. [4].

Recent findings suggest that sometimes a simple diaper swap won’t do the trick. Here are common signs it’s time to call a pediatrician or dermatologist: [1].

Once you've got your routine down, these diapers check the most boxes on the list above.

In a recent development, pampers is the only brand we found with two kinds of third-party validation across its sensitive-skin line. The newest, Pampers AMORE, is dermatologically accredited by the Skin Health Alliance and tested against more than 1,000 chemicals, according to Pampers’ product specifications. It’s hypoallergenic and free of fragrance, parabens, elemental chlorine, and latex. [5] Pampers Pure Protection carries the National Eczema Association’s Seal of Acceptance. [6] Pampers Swaddlers went fully fragrance-free across all sizes on June 22, 2026. [3] They are dermatologically tested and accredited by the Skin Health Alliance.

According to DYPER, the materials that touch baby’s skin are 100% plant-based, and the diaper has 55% USDA Certified Biobased content and is dermatologist-tested. [7].

Recent findings suggest that per Bambo Nature, the fluff pulp is totally chlorine-free (TCF), and the diapers contain no added substances known to be allergens or classified as skin irritants. [8].

In a recent development, huggies says Snug & Dry diapers are entirely fragrance-free, as well as free of lotions, parabens, and natural rubber latex. [9].

According to recent reports, per Honest, these diapers are OEKO-TEX Standard 100 certified (third-party tested for 350 harmful substances), dermatologist-tested, hypoallergenic, and fragrance-free. [10].

Recent findings suggest that what are the best diapers for a baby with sensitive skin? Look for diapers that are fragrance-free, hypoallergenic, and dermatologist-tested, ideally with third-party accreditation. Pampers Swaddlers (fragrance-free across all sizes since June 2026), Pampers Pure Protection (National Eczema Association Seal of Acceptance), and Pampers AMORE (Skin Health Alliance-accredited) all meet those criteria.

According to recent reports, what diapers do pediatric dermatologists recommend for sensitive or reactive skin? Rather than marketing words like “gentle” or “natural,” dermatologists prioritize independent validation, such as Skin Health Alliance accreditation or the National Eczema Association Seal of Acceptance. Those marks mean an outside organization has reviewed the product.

Sources indicate that what’s the best hypoallergenic diaper for a baby with eczema? The National Eczema Association’s Seal of Acceptance is the clearest outside marker for eczema-prone skin and, according to the NEA, Pampers Pure Protection at the moment carries it.

Sources indicate that what’s the best sensitive-skin diaper of 2026 for a baby with eczema? Pampers AMORE is the newest diaper built specifically for sensitive skin. Per Pampers, it’s accredited by the Skin Health Alliance, tested against more than 1000 chemicals, and free of fragrance, parabens, elemental chlorine, and latex.

Recent findings suggest that can switching diapers alone fix my baby’s eczema? No. A fragrance-free, hypoallergenic diaper helps, but routine matters as much or more: change every two to three hours, use barrier cream at every change, give daily diaper-free time, and clean gently. And since eczema is a chronic condition, your pediatrician should be part of the initiative.

Why does my baby’s rash only show up near the diaper elastic or leg cuffs? That pattern suggests a contact allergy to dye or elastic material rather than just general dermatitis. Have your pediatrician take a look.

Move Over, Potpourri – These 6 Fragrant Plants Fill a Room With Natural Christmas Scent

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance? The holidays are rich with aromas from pine-scented garlands to pumpkin pies baking in the oven, and using Christmas plants to bring another layer of perfume makes your home feel even more warm and inviting.

Sources indicate that while Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too. Alongside attractive greenery and beautiful blooms, these scented selections will add to the festive ambience.

Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.

It has been revealed that for a traditional Christmas fragrance with unique notes, rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) should be a staple for the holidays. This woody perennial herb is evergreen and has a piney aroma mixed with citrus, floral and mint notes that works so well with more traditional holiday scents. You could trim your potted rosemary like a topiary into a Christmas tree profile, or leave it in its natural bushy shape and pluck stems to tuck among roast potatoes or plunge into holiday cocktails.

In a recent development, while traditional rosemary is fabulous just as it is, other varieties can offer more in the way of holiday decor and still be used in the kitchen. Tuscan Blue rosemary, available from trees.com, has the same pleasing scent with particularly glossy leaves (and highly ornamental blue blooms in spring and summer). Arp rosemary, available from Burpee, has the strongest fragrance of all and while it's capable of growing into a major plant outside, it's easy to keep small in a pot.

In a recent development, provide a potted rosemary with bright light, ideally from a south-facing window, and potting soil that drains very well. Rosemary naturally grows in warm, dry climates but indoors it prefers cooler temperatures and a little more moisture, so just let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. This is a tough, adaptable plant so it can be grown outside year-round in zones 8-10, or simply pop it outdoors for spring and summer in colder zones.

In a recent development, forcing bulbs indoors is a fun holiday project and paperwhites (Narcissus papyraceus) are among the easiest to grow. The delicate white blooms resemble daffodils and grow elegantly on tall stems, with a floral fragrance that complements other seasonal scents well. Grown in a decorative dish or bowl, paperwhites offer sophisticated décor and delicious perfume in one.

Unlike other bulbs, narcissus don’t require a chill period so there's still time to get holiday blooms if you hurry, as it only takes three to six weeks to force paperwhite bulbs. A good bet are Ziva paperwhite bulbs, available from Eden Brothers, as they're effortlessly elegant and the easiest to grow. For a little more frill, Erlicheer paperwhite bulbs, also available from Eden Brothers, enjoy the same appealing fragrance and even more petals.

Use shallow containers with potting mix or glass dishes with decorative gravel, which allows you to see the bulbs and some of the roots as they grow. In zones 9-11, paperwhites can be replanted outdoors once they've finished flowering.

According to recent reports, for a floral perfume that carries the promise of spring, forced hyacinth bulbs are a must for the holidays. Hyacinths (Hyacinthus orientalis) smell intensely floral with notes of green growth, sweet honey and wholesome earthiness. As with paperwhites, you can grow these bulbs in containers with soil or use decorative glass containers to show off their interesting roots.

Bulbs need to be chilled for 10 to 14 weeks, then blooms takes three to four weeks to grow, so you'll need to buy pre-planted holiday hyacinths for flowers this year, which you'll find at some grocery stores as well as garden centers. But pop a note into your phone calendar now to remind yourself to plant hyacinth bulbs in September for bowls of fragrant Christmas flowers.

Sources indicate that once they bloom, keep your hyacinths in a cool spot to preserve the flowers for as long as possible. After flowering, you can replant bulbs outside in zones 4-8.

It has been revealed that cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’ is a variety of lemon cypress in a unique shade of yellow-green with a delicious citrus aroma. If you feel that holiday scents are sometimes a little too sweet and cloying, this is the plant you need to balance that with a fresh, clean perfume. As this evergreen is Christmas tree-shaped, lemon cypress adds a latest element to traditional holiday greenery too.

A great option for growing in a pot is the dwarf lemon cypress 'Wilma Goldcrest', available from trees.com. Though capable of eventually growing to 6 feet high and 1-2 feet wide, by growing this compact form in a planter, you can easily keep it small enough to bring indoors as a holiday houseplant for many years to come.

In a recent development, position lemon cypress where the foliage will be brushed against as this is how the aroma is released, or you can simply crush the foliage between finger and thumb for a fresh burst of fragrance whenever you fancy. Your lemon cypress will need bright light but fairly cool temperatures. Water the pot regularly to avoid total dryness, but don’t let the roots sit in soggy soil. This compact tree grows best outdoors so move it outside after the holidays in zones 7-11, or overwinter indoors as a houseplant in zones 3-6.

Scented geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) offer the ultimate opportunity to customize your holiday fragrance profile. There are varieties with foliage that smells like roses, citrus, apple, ginger, cinnamon, chocolate mint and even nutmeg. Mix and match or pair with other houseplants to concoct a signature Christmas scent.

It has been revealed that at this time of the year, the best place to find plants is via the Etsy scented geranium live plants hub which lists available stock from verified independent nurseries. You’ll get the most out of your scented geraniums by placing them where you can rub the leaves to release a burst of fragrance. They need a sunny spot, too, as well as soil that drains well. Water when the soil begins to dry and pinch back stems to keep the foliage dense.

Scented geraniums can be grown outdoors year-round in zones 10-11, while in cooler climates they're best treated as winter houseplants that enjoy the summer outside on a sunny patio.

For a unique chocolatey aroma, Oncidium Heaven Scent 'Redolence' is an orchid with a wonderfully sweet chocolate fragrance. You’ll also enjoy the elegant spikes of burgundy and white flowers that last for a month or more. Look out, too, for Oncidium Aka Baby 'Raspberry Chocolate' with a lighter but no less lovely chocolate perfume.

It's best to buy speciality orchids from specialist nurseries, and to be sure you’ll have aromatic flowers for the holidays, buy a plant that is already in bud or bloom. Akatsuka Orchid Gardens is one such nursery, based in Hawaii and stocking both the Heaven Scent 'Redolence' orchid and 'Raspberry Chocolate' orchid in bud and bloom. These orchids grow best in bright but indirect light and in a potting mix designed specifically for orchids. Water when the mix is dry and avoid overwatering or letting the mix get soggy. Good air circulation is also a must, and keep orchids as houseplants year-round.

A few simple practices will keep your aromatic holiday houseplants fresh and fragrant:.

For summers that feel like the inside of a diaper pail.

For when you’re too tired to do the squish test.

Why: Costco indicates its store brand is hypoallergenic and dermatologically tested for sensitive skin, and comes in 160-count boxes for Size 1.

Should I get a more absorbent or a more breathable diaper to prevent rash?

Both. Absorbency keeps wetness off skin, and breathability lets heat and humidity escape. Look for a diaper that does both.

Is a fragrance-free or an extra-absorbent diaper better for preventing diaper rash?

It has been revealed that you want both in one diaper. Fragrance-free cuts down on irritants, while absorbency handles the moisture behind a lot of rash.

Is it worth paying more for a rash-preventing diaper, and which one is best?

In a recent development, not necessarily. Frequent changes and barrier cream often matter more than price. Pampers Swaddlers is our top pick, backed by a Pampers-sponsored study showing 50% fewer instances of severe redness, at a mainstream price.

What’s the best rash-preventing diaper for a preemie with delicate skin?

Industry observers note that preemie skin needs extra-gentle materials, frequent changes, and clinician guidance before you switch products. Pampers says its Swaddlers Preemie diapers were developed with NICU nurses, are fragrance-free and hypoallergenic, and come in sizes P3 to P1 for babies under about 6 pounds.

Is a wetness-indicator diaper or an extra-absorbent diaper better for preventing rash?

Absorbency is what actually helps prevent rash. A wetness indicator is just a helpful reminder that it’s time to change.

School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this article is sponsored by Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI).
  • In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage.
  • Industry observers note that when my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this article is sponsored by Center for Science in the Public Interest (CSPI). Thank you for supporting the brands that support Motherly and mamas.

In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a latest building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school.

Industry observers note that when my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

It has been revealed that I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a substantial deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day?

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the blueprint because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by the USDA and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) every five years. When the DGA gets an upgrade, school nutrition standard changes will follow, as required by law.

Schools are right now implementing changes developed following the release of the 2020-2025 DGA. In April 2024, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA, formerly Food and Nutrition Service) , a government agency responsible for administering domestic nutrition programs, like the NSLP, issued a rule requiring schools to make changes to foods served at school, including:.

These updates join a comprehensive list of nutrition standards for school breakfasts and lunches that outline weekly serving requirements for fruits, vegetables, grains, meats and meat alternatives, and milk, as well as calorie minimums and maximums, and limits on saturated fat.

The USDA and HHS released the 2025-2030 DGA on January 7, 2026, triggering the next wave of school nutrition reviews in preparation for new recommendations and requirements. The USDA will compare the new DGA guidelines against existing school nutrition requirements, then draft a proposed rule on which schools, state agencies, advocates, industry experts, and consumer advocacy groups, like Center for the Science in the Public Interest, can provide feedback. The USDA will read and respond to comments, sometimes changing planned provisions in response to the feedback received, then publish its final rule.

At face value, this may seem like a good thing.

Sources indicate that the USDA and HHS appoints a Dietary Guidelines Advisory Committee (DGAC) every five years to serve as an independent, expert panel of scientists and researchers in nutrition, health and medicine. The committee spends years reviewing current nutrition science to write a scientific report that’s typically used as a foundational resource for new dietary guidelines. DGAs have historically followed the vast majority of the DGAC’s recommendations. But, as CSPI notes, USDA and HHS rejected more than half of the DGAC’s expert recommendations. Instead, the agencies, according to CSPI,  “hand-picked authors whose work aligned with beef, dairy, and protein supplement industry interests and the administration’s preconceived policy goals.”.

This group of hand-picked authors created a upcoming “Scientific Foundation for Dietary Guidelines for Americans,” which includes contradictory advice, recommending folks stick to prior, science-based saturated fat limits, while suggesting high-fat foods like whole milk and beef tallow are part of a healthy diet.

CSPI has raised other concerns about the 2025-2030 DGA, arguing that it gives harmful guidance to emphasize animal protein; advises people to consume double or more of the scientifically-backed recommendation for daily protein; reduces clarity around how people can eat a balanced diet within vegetable and protein categories; and adopts an inverted food pyramid that doesn’t accurately visually represent the dietary recommendations found within the text of the guidelines.

Recent findings suggest that as in cycles past, schools expect the USDA to use the most recent DGA as a guide to propose changes to school nutrition standards. It’s unclear exactly what changes will be put forth, but there will likely be a mix of nutrition wins and losses. It’s possible the new standards will reflect evidence-based nutrition guidance like increasing whole grains, protein, and whole fruit, and cutting back on added sugars, sodium, and refined grains in school meals.

However, it’s also likely the upcoming proposed standards may stray from evidence-based guidance by calling for decreased vegetable variety and overall fiber intake due to a deprioritization of plant-based proteins and an overemphasis on high-fat foods like whole milk and beef (rather than a variety of protein sources). For example, students could see more protein, like eggs and yogurt, at breakfast but miss out on a rainbow of vegetables and inclusive protein options like beans and tofu at lunch. Zooming out, meals lower in added sugars could be prioritized, while progress made on reducing saturated fat and sodium in school meals will be lost.

The best way to inform what your kids get on their breakfast and lunch trays at school is to make your voice heard. After proposing changes to nutrition standards, the government will open a public comment period where you can share your opinions about what should be included or excluded from school meals. When the proposed rule finally comes out, CSPI will make it easy to share your opinion through model comments and templates that will allow parents to comment directly on the proposed rule. Stay tuned for next steps by signing up for CSPI advocacy emails.

In a recent development, the regulatory red tape may seem overwhelming. That’s why non-profits like CSPI give parents tools to learn about school nutrition standards and enact change. To learn more about school nutrition standards, visit CSPI’s Healthier School Food advocacy page. If you’re ready to advocate for healthier school meals, check out CPSI’s Take Action page to get involved.

#136351. Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

Her friend died after giving birth. Now she’s writing legislation to save other moms

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1241 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change.
  • In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving.
  • Sources indicate that she never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mothering America is a regular column from Motherly and Chamber of Mothers sharing moms’ stories from across the country, showing the power of coming together to make change. Each piece is part of a larger effort to ensure every mother and family in the U.S. has the support and care to be well.

In 2008, Lauren Underwood was in graduate school at Johns Hopkins, earning a master’s in public health, when she met a woman with a big, bright smile named Shalon Irving.

Sources indicate that she never would have imagined the impact that friendship would have on her life’s work. Underwood would eventually become a U.S. representative for the state of Illinois, fighting to protect moms like Irving, who died before she could see her friend take office.

Industry observers note that at the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

Sources indicate that the two—Rep. Underwood, a registered nurse, and Irving, an epidemiologist—stayed in touch through the years. In January 2017, Rep. Underwood served as a senior advisor at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, and Irving worked for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She had also given birth to a beautiful baby girl named Soleil.

In a recent development, three weeks later, though, Irving wasn’t feeling well. “She went to the doctor several times, explaining that something wasn’t right,” Rep. Underwood remembers. On January 28, Irving died of complications related to high blood pressure. She was 36.

Industry observers note that “Shalon had a career focused on ending health disparities, and she was so excited to become a mom,” Rep. Underwood notes.

Today, Rep. Underwood is the architect of a series of 14 bills called the Momnibus, which was reintroduced to Congress this spring. The Momnibus addresses “every clinical and non-clinical factor” leading to preventable maternal deaths and disparities in this country; it’s evidence-based, data-driven, and offers states, communities, providers, and nonprofits the resources to help save moms like Irving’s lives. For Rep. Underwood, the Momnibus is personal.

While a member of Congress, Rep. Underwood is also a woman and a friend who, like too many in this country, lost a dear friend and felt a fire to make change.

Rep. Underwood recalls Irving’s funeral as devastating—particularly because many of those in attendance held positions of the highest authority in public health in this country. She remembers the head of the CDC speaking at Irving’s funeral and expressing bewilderment at her death.

For Rep. Underwood, it was no mystery why mothers like Irving die in childbirth and shortly thereafter. As a clinician, she had seen firsthand health disparities in action; as a Black woman, maternal mortality was an unfortunate “phenomenon where it’s just so common when you talk about the maternal crisis.”.

In a recent development, today, we know about 84 percent of pregnancy-related deaths like Irving’s are preventable—meaning that most of the moms who aren’t here today should be here, and could be here, with the proper supports in place. Black moms are more than three times as likely to die in pregnancy or the postpartum months than white women—a disparity that persists across income and education levels.

According to recent reports, “People think higher education or higher income is protective. They think that if you are a healthcare worker, you’re going to get the best healthcare. If you know the risks, are self-aware, confident, and have agency, and you can speak up for yourself, then these kinds of things won’t happen to you. Shalon and her death fly in the face of all of those assumptions, and it breaks your heart.”.

When she made the decision to run for Congress, Rep. Underwood knew that if she won, maternal mortality would be an matter she’d work on.

In 2018, Rep. Underwood became the youngest Black woman ever elected to Congress. She teamed up with Rep. Alma Adams (D-NC), who also had personal experience with maternal health: Adams’ daughter had experienced a very challenging labor and delivery, known in medical terms as severe maternal morbidity, or an experience that has lasting impacts on a mother’s health.

Together, in April 2019, the two formed the Black Maternal Health Caucus. At a crowded press conference, Rep. Underwood fought back tears. “To be in this moment with the dome of the Capitol behind us and these cameras and people asking questions and it’s this diverse, multi-generational, multi-ethnic, male and female moment of speaking about an matter that was so personal to me—I was just overcome,” she claims. “It was a moment of power and resolve. It was an invitation. We were planting a flag, saying, ‘We’re here. We’re going to do this work. We know that there’s an opportunity to bring change.’”.

In a recent development, rep. Underwood didn’t expect the Black Maternal Health Caucus to grow into one of the largest bipartisan caucuses on the Hill. “We left that press conference and our phones started ringing, and it never stopped.”.

Rep. Underwood has dedicated her career to ensuring everyone—moms included—has equitable healthcare so we can all feel our best. She’s also dedicated her career to ending the maternal mortality crisis. “We know exactly what to do. We just need to invest, have the resolve, and to say, ‘This is unacceptable. Let’s fix this issue.’”.

Sources indicate that she also reminds us that Congress works on the issues that members raise. “If a Member comes in and claims, ‘This is notable to my community, and this is an essential issue that we tackle,’ that’s how solutions advance.” Many of her ideas for bills, she says, come from your stories.

“Often, people think that their story doesn’t matter, and when they come in to advocate, they think they need to have statistics or be a walking encyclopedia,” Rep. Underwood states. “But we are in a relationship business, and connection is currency. The fastest way to build a connection is to share your humanity, tell your story, and invite space for that vulnerability.”.

What that means for you: If you have a story to share, Members of Congress are home in their districts through the end of the month, with offices open Monday through Friday and available for meetings. (Not sure how to set up a meeting? Check out Chamber of Mothers’ ‘Moms at Recess’ guide, which includes step-by-step plans and tips for hosting a meeting with Members of Congress.).

Rep. Underwood also underscores the importance of being loud about solutions and progress in maternal health. She highlights the power of doulas, lactation consultants, and community support in maternal health—and the fact that, to date, one of the Momnibus’ 14 bills has been signed into law. Others have passed the House. The Momnibus has also unlocked more than $250 million for states, community organizations, researchers, and providers to save lives. (You can find out which projects are being funded with Momnibus dollars in your community through the Caucus’s Momnibus Money Tracker.).

“We want the news of a pregnancy to be a time of joy and hope and eager anticipation and wonder,” Rep. Underwood notes. “This can’t just be a conversation around problems. We want people to know that we’re working on this, that we have their backs, and about the opportunities, help, and the resources that are available.”.

No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste.
  • According to recent reports, over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away.
  • Some plants actually prefer leaner soil.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

According to recent reports, over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

Some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the upcoming plants a little boost.

Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

Nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

Moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

Grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

In a recent development, sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

Industry observers note that the most vital part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

Hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

Recent findings suggest that hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

Calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

Like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

Sources indicate that while cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

While all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

Sources indicate that remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

Remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

One pick per real-life diaper disaster, from the newborn days to the crawl-away-mid-change era.

Forty years ago, parents had two diaper choices: cloth or disposable. That was kind of it. Now, we have the internet and Reddit opinions and TikTok influencers telling us which diapers they swear by. The list is endless and ripe for an endless 3 a.m. scroll.

According to recent reports, fortunately, you don’t need a PhD in absorbent polymers to pick a diaper; you just need the right one for your baby’s actual problem. So, we ranked the best baby diapers of 2026 by situation.

Industry observers note that the verdict: The best everyday diaper for newborns and beyond... the easiest “just buy this”.

The verdict: The best blowout fix for a baby who treats changes like a contact sport.

The verdict: A nighttime diaper for babies who soak through before morning.

The verdict: A fragrance-free premium pick for skin that reacts to everything.

What’s the best subscription diaper proposal for the money?

Should I use a premium or budget diaper if my baby’s in daycare full-time?

Industry observers note that budget diapers can handle daytime. In Consumer Reports’ 2026 testing, its budget Value Pick scored as high on absorption and dryness as its top performer. Many parents opt for budget during the day and premium for overnight.

Is a thinner or thicker diaper better for an active, cruising toddler?

A slimmer core with a flexible waistband (like Pampers Cruisers 360 Fit) tends to give busy babies more freedom of movement without losing all-crucial absorbency.

How often should I change a newborn’s diaper to prevent rash?

Changing diapers every 2 to 3 hours and using barrier ointment is the main way to prevent diaper rash, per AAP. If a rash won’t clear up, bleeds, or looks like an allergic reaction, call your pediatrician or dermatologist.

Do I really need a different diaper for day versus night?

Not always, but heavy wetters often do. Separate day and night diapers are an increasingly common fix for overnight soakers. Pampers AMORE, rolled out in March 2026, is billed by Pampers as its most absorbent diaper, in sizes Newborn-7.

Sources indicate that our four kittens â one female, three males â lost their mommy just after they turned two months old. They were already raiding her food bowl to munch on her dry kibble. Since mommy passed away from mastitis, they have developed a habit of trying to suckle on one another. I have seen each kitten do this.

We tried to separate them as soon as we see them doing this, but nothing works.

Recent findings suggest that what can we do to help stop this? â.

It has been revealed that I am so sorry these babies lost their mama so suddenly. They have essentially decided, âNo Mom? Fine, weâll improvise!â.

What you are seeing is called non-nutritive suckling, and in orphaned kittens, it can be surprisingly persistent. It is not necessarily hunger at this age. Suckling is also a built-in comfort behavior, and losing their mother can leave them looking for another way to satisfy that need. Research in orphaned kittens has specifically documented cross-suckling between littermates, with a higher risk in kittens that lost their mother.

Recent findings suggest that rather than simply trying to stop the behavior, you could give them an appropriate place to redirect it. There has been research into providing a âsurrogate motherâ for orphaned kittens, essentially a soft plush object fitted with artificial nipples, sometimes described as a kitten pacifier or nursing station. The idea is lovely because it gives them an outlet for that very normal suckling drive while allowing the siblings to continue enjoying their key social contact. I would look for a purpose-designed kitten nursing surrogate or a very soft, durable, washable object specifically intended for this use, rather than improvising with anything that could shed fibers, unravel, or be swallowed.

It is also worth knowing that some cats never completely give up their âbaby habit.â Suckling can persist into adulthood and may be directed toward blankets, clothing, plastics, themselves, siblings, or other cats, and even towards the owners. In many cats, it is simply a comforting ritual, but it becomes a concern if they chew and swallow fabric or fur, or if another cat develops irritated or injured skin. So for these four little characters, the goal does not necessarily have to be âstop suckling forever.â It is more about teaching them, âHere is your approved place to do that.â.

Sources indicate that most importantly, keep an eye on the areas they are right now targeting. Suckling around the belly or especially the genital area can cause significant irritation and injury, so those kittens should be separated from the suckler when necessary and examined for redness, swelling, hair loss, wounds, or difficulty urinating.

With a safe alternative, plenty of play and enrichment, and gentle redirection, they may gradually outgrow the behavior, or they may simply become those adult cats who still insist on having their favorite comfort blanket. Some cats do have a talent for keeping their childhood traditions!

Industry observers note that chloe Bridges is an actress with a career spanning film and television. A Columbia University graduate, she welcomed her first child, her son Beau, with her husband, actor and comedian Adam Devine, in February 2024.

A bad day today doesn’t mean a bad day tomorrow. Everything is just constantly changing and in flux.

According to recent reports, dr. Chambers: The first lesson was really that I just can’t do it all by myself. I take pride in being able to accomplish things, and I am so proud of the things I have accomplished, professionally, personally. But motherhood is not one of those things where there’s a badge of honor when you suffer. So I had to learn, from the newborn phase to the late infancy phase to now, that I need help. Sometimes I need help because I can’t be in two places at once. Sometimes I need help because I don’t feel well. Sometimes I need help because I need to be restored, and I need a break. In a recent development, dr. Chambers: RSV, or respiratory syncytial virus, is a highly contagious respiratory infection that can get really serious for our youngest babies. When we think about the seasonality of it, it tends to run during the fall and winter months, and the seriousness is that it can lead to hospitalization. It can lead to infant mortality. Babies can get really, really exhausted and tired, and that noisy type of rapid breathing, those are all red flags that something is wrong. These are not all the possible symptoms of RSV in infants, so it’s notable to talk to your doctor. If you notice any symptoms in your baby, talk to your baby’s doctor right away.

If eligible, pregnant women may have the power to help protect their babies by choosing to get vaccinated with ABRYSVO® (Respiratory Syncytial Virus Vaccine), Pfizer’s respiratory syncytial virus vaccine that’s given during 32 through 36 weeks of pregnancy to help protect babies against RSV infection from birth through 6 months during September through January in most of the United States.

According to recent reports, to avoid the potential risk of preterm birth, ABRYSVO should be given during 32 through 36 weeks gestational age. The most common side effects in pregnant women are injection site pain, headaches, muscle pain, and nausea. Low birth weight and jaundice can also occur in infants. Dr. Chambers: Many moms don’t realize that they are constantly making antibodies to things they’re exposed to and passing those antibodies onto their babies naturally. Maternal immunization is an vital part of my prenatal care discussions because babies are at highest risk of infection from RSV during their first three months of life.

Chloe: I want him to see me as competent and capable, but I also want him to see me as playful and fun. I think that’s been a major part of it. Maybe especially having a little boy, I want to be playful with him, and I want him to be able to have that kind of relationship with me. The nurturing comes so easy, but the playfulness has come a little harder. I hope he looks back and he’s like, ‘You know what? We had fun.’.

Chambers: I hope my son sees me as someone he can trust, as someone who can give him advice, as someone who always makes decisions that are grounded in love and goodness, and someone who’s been making decisions since before he was born to set him up to have the best possible life.
