📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse are fast becoming the it couple of the moment (not least of all because the man formerly known as Edward Cullen is now Bond, James Bond). So you'd best believe they're setting trends left, right, and center – even in the world of indoor gardening.

Sources indicate that and while we'd expect the pair to have a suitably impressive garden, it turns out their houseplant of choice is considerably more interesting than your average monstera or spider plant. In fact, it's a miniature tree with a rather sophisticated reputation: the not-so-humble bonsai!

Yes, with the couple's busy schedules taking them between different homes and locations, it makes sense that they're all about the idea of bringing greenery indoors. After all, houseplants offer a lovely way to make a space feel personal, even when you're not necessarily putting down roots for the long term. And if you're going to invest in an indoor plant, then why not make it something a little more unusual?

Speaking to the Perfectly Imperfect Newsletter in September 2024, Suki Waterhouse revealed that she developed a rather unexpected obsession with bonsai trees during the final month of her pregnancy.

Recent findings suggest that 'When I was preggers in the last month and didn’t really feel like seeing anyone, I got obsessed with getting a bonsai tree,' she says. 'I found a number on Google and pulled up to a house in East Hollywood and a lady had a bunch of them locked up in her back garden. Felt super cool and mysterious. Some of them she’d had for 30 years. Fell in love with this guy and have become obsessed with pruning.'.

The leaves on this bonsai fold up at night or in subdued light, and it wakes up when we do!

It's a wonderfully specific plant obsession, and one we can absolutely get behind. Especially as there's something rather magical about a tiny tree that's been carefully cultivated for decade; there's a reason that bonsai is as much an art form as it is a gardening hobby.

Of course, Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson aren't the only ones who appreciate the appeal of the beautiful bonsai tree. In fact, there's been something of a growing appreciation for the slower, more mindful side of gardening, and bonsai? Why, that fits the philosophy rather beautifully.

Recent findings suggest that more importantly? Well, despite the fact that bonsai trees have a reputation for being (whisper it) high-maintenance, they're not as intimidating as their appearance might suggest. The trick is choosing the right one – so look for a variety suited to indoor conditions and make a note of its basic requirements. And, as Suki herself pointed out, a little regular pruning and thoughtful watering can go a long way.

If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have inspired you to introduce a little bonsai magic into your own home, there are a few varieties worth considering...

Recent findings suggest that if you're new to bonsai, ficus is arguably the best place to start. These tropical trees are considerably more forgiving than many traditional bonsai varieties and adapt well to indoor conditions. Their glossy leaves and interesting roots make them particularly striking, too.

Give something like this Small Ficus Live Bonsai Tree from Brussell's Bonsai a bright position with plenty of indirect light, keep it away from cold draughts and water when the top layer of compost begins to dry.

If Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson have got you in the mood for something a little more unusual, consider the Hawaiian umbrella tree (Schefflera arboricola).

This bonsai's distinctive leaves and naturally branching growth make it a particularly attractive choice for an indoor plant.

Sources indicate that it's also relatively tolerant of indoor humidity levels and can cope with slightly less-than-perfect light conditions, although a bright spot will always help it thrive. Take care to allow the soil to dry slightly between waterings, and prune regularly to maintain its shape.

A lovely option for anyone who tends to be a little forgetful with watering, jade bonsai (Crassula ovata) is a succulent that enjoys plenty of bright light and needs much less frequent watering than tropical bonsai varieties.

Pick up something like this Live Jade from Brussell's Bonsai, let the compost dry out thoroughly between waterings, and make sure it's planted in a free-draining bonsai mix to prevent its roots from sitting in excess moisture.

Sources indicate that of course, even the most beginner-friendly bonsai isn't quite a plant you can forget about. Even Robert Pattinson and Suki Waterhouse will tell you, light, watering and occasional pruning are all crucial, and it's worth remembering that not every bonsai is suited to indoor living.

As a general rule of thumb, tropical and subtropical varieties are generally the best choice for growing inside; most traditional temperate trees need to experience the changing seasons outdoors.

Still, there's something rather lovely about the idea of tending to a little tree that could stay with you for decades. And if Suki Waterhouse's experience is anything to go by, it might just become your next very absorbing, very cool, very mysterious hobby.

Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend plans to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

Welcome to our "Ask Dr. Paola" series, where every other Monday we bring expert advice straight from Dr. Paola Cuevas (MVZ) to help our readers better understand their cat's health and well-being. Whether you're a upcoming pet parent or a seasoned cat lover, Dr. Paola is here to provide answers to your most pressing questions. From nutrition tips and preventive care to troubleshooting common behavioral challenges, Dr. Paola is ready to offer insights that will keep your kitty happy, healthy, and feline fine. Stay tuned for expert guidance on a range of topics that matter most to you and your cat, so you can make informed decisions and provide the best possible care for your furry companion. â.

Haveâ a âquestion? Send it in here!

My cat, Mitzi, is 16 years and 8 months old. She has early-stage kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, which she is on medication for. About 2 months ago, she became deaf, and since then has refused to leave the master bedroom. I have moved her water bowl and litter box there and feed her there.

Is there anything I can do to get her to come out?â.

At her age, sweet Mitzi has certainly earned the right to enjoy her golden years at her own pace, but I can imagine it is difficult to see her withdraw from the rest of the house, especially when you remember how she used to move around. However, I would not necessarily interpret her reluctance to leave the bedroom as something we need to correct. Losing her hearing can be quite disorienting. Imagine walking into a room where you can no longer hear footsteps, familiar voices, or the little sounds that help you understand what is happening around you. For Mitzi, the bedroom may now feel like her safest little world, where everything is familiar and predictable.

I actually think you have done a wonderful job adapting her environment by bringing her food, water, and litter box closer. Rather than encouraging her to leave right away, I would focus on helping her feel confident enough to explore if she wishes. You could start by sitting with her near the bedroom doorway, offering a favorite treat or a little affection. Gradually place treats a short distance beyond the door, allowing her to decide whether she wants to investigate.

According to recent reports, take care to only approach her within her visual field, avoid startling her while she sleeps, and keep pathways clear and nonslip. Think of it as extending her newly introduced world one comfortable step at a time, rather than asking her to return to her old routine.

In a recent development, there is one thing I would not overlook, though. Mitzi has both chronic kidney disease and hyperthyroidism, and at her age, reduced mobility or withdrawal can also be associated with arthritis, high blood pressure, visual changes, or inadequate control of her thyroid disease. I would recommend a senior cat veterinary checkup that includes blood pressure measurement, assessment for arthritis, and follow-up kidney and thyroid testing. Sometimes what looks like a behavioral change is actually a senior cat quietly telling us that they are in pain and something does not feel quite right.

In a recent development, most importantly, please do not feel that you are encouraging a bad habit by keeping her essentials in the bedroom. You are adapting her home to meet her changing needs, and that is a beautiful expression of your love and care for her. If the bedroom is where Mitzi feels safe, eats well, drinks, uses her litter box, and enjoys your tech giant, that can be a perfectly good quality of life.

At this stage, happiness is not measured by how much of the house she explores, but by how comfortable and secure she feels in the little world she chooses.

In a recent development, every time the topic of vaccines comes up, thereâs always someone who questions whether our pets really need them. Recent findings suggest that rabies is a perfect example. This is not some historical disease or something that only affects animals in remote areas or underdeveloped countries. It can infect mammals, including our own cats, dogs, and even us. Whatâs even scarier is that once the clinical signs appear, rabies is almost always fatal, making prevention essential.

Recent events in Quebec offer a timely reminder. Amid an emerging wildlife outbreak, three domestic cats tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies in 2026. Although these numbers pale in comparison to the number of infected wildlife recorded since December 20241, it demonstrates how a disease circulating in wild animals can reach our pets.

And this isn't just a Canadian concern. Rabies variants and wildlife risks differ by region, but keeping pets appropriately vaccinated is a responsibility shared by pet parents everywhere.

Despite its name, raccoon-strain rabies isn't exclusive to raccoons; they are simply the reservoir species of this particular variant of the rabies virus. Skunks and other mammals â including cats â can also become infected.

Rabies attacks the central nervous system. It spreads mainly through the bite of an infected animal, when virus-containing saliva enters the body. Saliva can also transmit the virus if it reaches an open wound, the eyes, nose, or mouth.

In a recent development, raccoon rabies had been eliminated in Quebec following an outbreak between 2006 and 2009, but the virus resurfaced in 2024. Since then, more outbreaks have appeared, and case numbers have climbed sharply in 2026, particularly in MontÃ©rÃ©gie. By October 29, 328 animals had tested positive for raccoon-strain rabies across the province. The three infected cats are examples of how a virus circulating in wildlife can also reach our pets, even though cats are not the main reservoir responsible for spreading this variant.

Recent findings suggest that cats are naturally curious, territorial predators. They investigate unfamiliar scents, watch moving animals, explore hidden spaces, and sometimes pursue creatures that would be better left alone. These behaviors are normal expressions of feline biology, not evidence that a cat is being reckless.

Unfortunately, wildlife encounters can turn dangerous very quickly. A raccoon searching for food near a house may cross paths with an outdoor cat. A skunk hiding beneath a shed may be investigated by a curious feline. Even a sick or disoriented wild animal can catch a cat's attention, and one of the hallmarks of rabies infection in wild animals is a reduced fear of humans and predators as the infection attacks the nervous system. And cats being cats, curiosity can get them into trouble! These encounters don't just happen deep in the woods. A backyard, garage, or garden fence can be enough.

In a recent development, one of the infected cats was believed to have contracted rabies after contact with a wild animal. Another case led to three people receiving preventive treatment following possible exposure.

Rabies doesn't always turn an animal into a movie villain, either. Early signs can be subtle, which is why recognizing unusual behavior and reporting possible exposure is so important.

Recent findings suggest that when people think of rabies, they often picture a snarling animal, dripping saliva, and attacking everything in sight. Hollywood certainly loves that version! Unfortunately, rabies doesn't always come with such obvious special effects.

Sources indicate that in cats, the first signs can be surprisingly subtle. A normally friendly kitty may suddenly become grumpy, hide more than usual, vocalize differently, lose interest in food, or behave in ways that seem completely out of character. Since cats are already experts at keeping their humans guessing, a sudden behavior change can sometimes be easy to dismiss. But when a cat starts acting noticeably different from their usual, wonderfully weird self, it's worth paying attention.

As the disease progresses, neurological signs become more apparent. Affected cats may become disoriented, walk unsteadily, have difficulty swallowing, drool excessively, develop weakness, or eventually become paralyzed. Some become unusually aggressive or sensitive to touch, sounds, and light.

Sources indicate that there is also a less dramatic presentation called paralytic rabies, sometimes referred to as âdumb rabiesâ. Instead of becoming aggressive, affected animals may become unusually quiet, weak, or withdrawn. Difficulty swallowing, a drooping jaw, and progressive paralysis can follow. So no, a rabid animal doesn't necessarily look like it's auditioning for a horror movie.

Industry observers note that of course, these signs can also occur with other neurological conditions, injuries, and intoxications. Nobody should attempt to diagnose rabies based on behavior alone. A cat showing sudden, unexplained neurological changes needs prompt veterinary attention, particularly if wildlife exposure is possible.

Here's another catch: rabies can take weeks, sometimes even months, to show itself. A cat may seem perfectly fine after an encounter with an infected animal, but that doesn't mean the virus isn't already in its body. So if a possible exposure happens, don't wait for your cat to look sick before calling the vet. By then, it may be too late.

Sadly, once rabies reaches the clinical stage, there is no cure, and the outcome is almost always fatal. That's why a suspected exposure should never be a wait-and-see situation. Don't wait for signs to appear; contact your veterinarian right away. With rabies, prevention isn't just better than treatment; it's our best chance to protect our cats in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that think your indoor cat doesn't need a rabies vaccine? Think again! Indoor cats have fewer opportunities to encounter wildlife, but escapes happen, doors get left open, and sometimes wildlife finds its way indoors. Nobody plans these little adventures, least of all the cat!

It has been revealed that rabies vaccination is also required by law for cats in many countries and jurisdictions. Even where it isn't mandatory, keeping your cat vaccinated is an important part of preventive care. Ask your veterinarian about the appropriate schedule for your cat.

Sources indicate that and remember, vaccination doesn't mean ignoring a possible exposure. If your vaccinated cat is bitten by a potentially rabid animal, contact your veterinarian right away.

If your cat is bitten or scratched by a wild animal, contact your veterinarian immediately, even if your cat seems perfectly fine. Bite wounds can hide beneath all that lovely fur, and waiting for signs to appear is not an option.

Keep your cat away from other animals and don't try to catch or handle the wild animal. Report suspicious wildlife to local authorities and let trained professionals deal with it.

If a person is bitten or scratched, or infected saliva enters an open wound or contacts the eyes, nose, or mouth, wash the area thoroughly with soap and running water for 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately. Post-exposure treatment can prevent rabies from developing, so don't delay.

According to recent reports, and please, leave dead wildlife alone. No bare-handed investigations or impromptu rescue missions!

Quebec is also fighting the outbreak through wildlife surveillance and vaccination campaigns using vaccine baits. These efforts help protect wild animals and reduce further spread.

In a recent development, cats will be cats. A rustling bush can become the most fascinating thing in the universe, and a passing raccoon may look like an invitation to investigate. We can't blame them for being curious. We can give them safer ways to enjoy their adventures.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, all year, I save up bubble wrap to use as a cheap DIY solution to see my garden through the winter. My trick is simple: I sandwich bubble wrap between a folded rectangle of burlap and wrap it around patio pots. Those little pockets of air act as excellent insulation, but my burlap and bubble-wrap pot-cozy does so much more than help to keep borderline-tender plants alive through winter.

In a recent development, if you're a fan of container gardening, you'll know that the temperature of soil in planters is so much more erratic than in the ground, leaving roots riding a right rollercoaster of conditions. By insulating pots, I save my plants a whole heap of stress, which means they can use their precious energy for far more exciting things. Winter-flowering pansies and violas in pots can stall in a cold snap, but stop that soil from freezing solid around their shallow roots and the plants will carry on pushing out their cheery petals. Winter-flowering heather in planters, too, will bloom far more steadily if their root balls are protected.

Industry observers note that A DIY pot-wrap also helps to stop plants from drying out. When soil freezes – and it’ll freeze far sooner and deeper in a planter than in the ground – roots can’t access its moisture. If the plant keeps losing water through its leaves (and remember the wind strips moisture from foliage just as readily as the sun), it’s no different to drought conditions. And when a plant is losing more water than it can replace, it goes into survival mode. For early-flowering shrubs like Daphne odora and ornamental camellias, that can mean dropped buds and zero blooms.

Sources indicate that wrapping also helps to stop pots from cracking in the continual freeze-thaw of winter, especially if they're made from porous terracotta. And let’s not forget those borderline-hardy plants either: with their roots already safely insulated in bubble wrap and burlap in late fall, it’s a super-quick job to zip up shrubs in frost jackets when a cold spell is forecast.

Industry observers note that it’s best to combine bubble wrap with good-quality, tightly-woven burlap on a roll such as this from Walmart to insulate pots. Cut a rectangle of burlap that’s twice the height of the pot and long enough to wrap all the way around with a generous overlap. Then fold the burlap in two and lay bubble wrap in between the two layers. Tie this around the pot with heavy-duty twine or rope, being careful not to cover the soil surface.

There are so many other uses for these low-cost materials as we head into winter:.

Bubble wrap is so useful when winterizing your garden and, covered with a layer of burlap, looks pretty smart. I like to tie red ribbon around for the holidays, too, and my winter protection looks like Christmas decor! Re-using materials in your garden, whether you're recycling cardboard as a mulch or trying a few DIY upcycling projects to upgrade your garden storage, makes your garden budget go further, too.

This feature is part of the Weekend Wins series, packed with quick and easy gardening tasks that bring a massive reward.

A homemade pebble tray is the no-cost solution that brings larger, lusher houseplant leaves through winter.

Catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Nobody enjoys thinking about serious illness in a pet, and itâs natural to want to look the other way. But considering many serious feline health conditions respond well to early intervention, a little knowledge can go a long way. Here are eight of the most serious, what they tend to look like, and practical steps that can help lower the risk. The aim isnât to worry anyone, just to help owners feel prepared.

It has been revealed that heart problems are notoriously hard to spot in cats, even during a routine health check, because the usual signs, like a murmur, donât always show up during an exam. The most common form of cardiac disease â hypertrophic cardiomyopathy â causes the heart muscle to thicken so it canât work as well, and it can cause sudden death. Vets rely on heart scans, chest X-rays, and blood tests to discover heart disease.

In a recent development, lowering the risk: Genetics play a massive part, so anyone buying a kitten from a breeder should ask whether the parentsâ hearts have been checked, particularly if your breed of choice is one with a higher incidence of cardiac disease, like purebred Maine Coons, Siamese, Sphynx, Ragdoll, and Burmese. A high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet formulated for cats is a vital ingredient in promoting heart health. Cat food must contain the amino acid taurine because cats cannot make it themselves, and a diet lacking this essential nutrient is a fast track to heart disease.

Kidney disease is common in older cats. The kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter waste, which highlights up as drinking and urinating more, tiredness, weight loss, and a scruffy coat. It can also lead to high blood pressure and low red blood cell counts, which cause pale gums, weakness, and fast breathing.

Lowering the risk: Although kidney disease canât be entirely prevented, regular checkups with blood and urine tests can catch changes early. A balanced diet helps, and maximizing a catâs water intake by feeding wet food and providing a range of enticing water options can make a significant difference.

According to recent reports, feline Leukemia Virus (FeLV) is prevalent in cat populations around the world and is the most common cause of feline cancer. FeLV attacks the bone marrow, and the clinical signs of infection can be quite variable, but often include lethargy, weight loss, poor appetite, and weakness. Because FeLV cripples the immune system, affected cats are more susceptible to disease, and an otherwise simple infection can be deadly.

It has been revealed that lowering the risk: Vaccination is the best protection. Keeping cats indoors and away from possibly infected cats helps, as does quarantining newcomers and regularly cleaning dishes, toys, bedding, and litter boxes.

In a recent development, this is the most common hormone disease in cats, affecting about 10% of cats over age ten. It can lead to heart problems, kidney disease, blindness, and death. Cats lose weight rapidly despite a huge appetite, and some suddenly go blind because of high blood pressure. Fortunately, the outlook is good with treatment, including medication, surgery, or radioactive iodine.

Lowering the risk: Hyperthyroidism canât be prevented, so spotting changes early and getting annual blood screening are the best weapons.

According to recent reports, up to one in a hundred cats develops diabetes in their lifetime, either because they donât make enough insulin or canât use it properly. Left untreated, it can cause serious complications. Signs include weight loss, drinking and urinating more, accidents outside the litter box, and bloody urine. Treatment is usually insulin injections, but if caught early, it can sometimes be managed through diet.

Lowering the risk: Feeding a high-quality, nutritionally balanced diet with low carbohydrate levels can help reduce the risks. The most common form of diabetes in cats is Type 2 (insulin resistance) and the best way to avoid this disease is by maintaining a lean, healthy body condition.

Rabies is almost always fatal, and cats are the domestic animal most likely to get it. It spreads through bites and scratches, often from wildlife such as bats, skunks, raccoons, and foxes. Some infected cats become withdrawn, others irritable or aggressive, and drooling and wide pupils are common. It is dangerous for people too.

In a recent development, lowering the risk: Vaccines protect for one to three years. If contact with rabies is suspected, veterinary attention must be sought immediately. The disease is invariably fatal once clinical signs of rabies appear, so donât wait.

It has been revealed that feline Infectious Peritonitis (FIP) is caused by a mutated form of feline coronavirus. Early signs are mild, such as tiredness, but many cats develop a swollen belly from fluid, and it can progress fast. Until recently, FIP was almost always fatal, though newer treatments are changing this.

Industry observers note that lowering the risk: Good hygiene between cats and isolating newcomers until theyâre healthy reduce exposure. Keeping cats healthy and up to date on other vaccines may also help.

Spread by mosquitoes, heartworms are less common in cats than in dogs, but they can still cause serious disease, including sudden death. Wheezing and coughing are the most common signs, and the infection is hard to detect.

Lowering the risk: A monthly preventive is the best defense. If you live in an area where heartworm is present, it takes only one mosquito, so even indoor cats can be exposed.

Sources indicate that not every disease on this list can be prevented, but many can be avoided or managed simply by providing your cat with a high-quality diet and keeping up with regular vet checks. Blood and urine tests, appropriate vaccines, and monthly flea, tick, and heartworm protection all help, and keeping cats indoors lowers exposure to injury and illness. Catching problems early is often what makes treatment most effective, and a vet can help tailor a blueprint for each cat.

June 2020 was a challenging time for Kelly. She had recently lost her mother, leaving her in a state of grief, and in an attempt to find solace and cope with her loss, she took up running. It was during one of these runs, only her second, that a tiny, fragile kitten crossed her path.

Recent findings suggest that kelly was jogging past vast cornfields, and her mind was hyper-focused on the pleasing sound of the stalks rustling in the wind when a small calico kitten appeared out of the blue. She was alone, sick, and desperately in need of help.

Snickers, as she would later be christened, was in terrible shape. Her eyes were crusted shut; she couldn't meow, and she had severe respiratory challenges, including sneezing. Her frail body was covered in fleas, and it was clear she was suffering.

In a recent development, moved by compassion, Kelly scooped up the little kitten and carried her the two miles back to her home, where she was given a much-needed bath and plenty of TLC. The following day, Kelly took her to the local veterinarian, who ran various tests and initiated a series of treatments.

Sources indicate that despite the efforts of the local vet, the situation didn't improve, and the bills were mounting. Snickers' condition was dire.

Despite the financial strain, Kelly's determination to save Snickers was unwavering. After several trips to the vet, it became clear that this brave little kitten needed specialized care. Snickers was referred to a specialist in Louisville, Kentucky, two hours away. There, a CT scan revealed the root of her health issues: large polyps behind her eyes and deep within her inner ear.

The specialist recommended two major surgeries to remove the polyps. The surgeries were spaced six weeks apart and were extremely expensive. The first surgery was a great success, but the second operation had a life-altering consequence. During the procedure, one of the polyps slipped into her neck, temporarily cutting off oxygen to the brain. She essentially died for a few seconds before the surgical team managed to resuscitate her with CPR. Tragically, Snickers woke up from the operation blind.

Recent findings suggest that the prognosis was uncertain, with a 50/50 chance of her regaining her eyesight. But Kelly, determined and resolute, refused to give up on her beloved feline companion. She watched over Snickers as she adjusted to her newfound blindness, never losing hope.

Remarkably, a couple of months later, a miracle occurred. One day, while she was waving something in front of Snickers, the catâs reaction gave Kelly a glimmer of hope. It appeared that Snickers might be regaining her eyesight. Ecstatic about this newfound possibility, Kelly promptly took Snickers back to the specialist, who confirmed the miraculous news: Snickers had indeed regained her eyesight.

Industry observers note that now, Snickers is a thriving and healthy six-year-old cat, bearing her distinctive, always-smiling face. Latest Update: Want To Befriend a Squirrel? Here's How To Attract These Cute Critters To Your Yard and Earn Their Trust

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1408 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You don't have to be a Disney princess to befriend a squirrel, which is good news for anyone who's long been keen to woo one of these cute critters themselves (ideally without a Snow White-level singsong).
  • Recent findings suggest that look, I'll level with you; I know that squirrels might not be everyone's favorite garden visitors.
  • Yes, squirrels can actually play a surprisingly useful role in the garden and wider ecosystem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You don't have to be a Disney princess to befriend a squirrel, which is good news for anyone who's long been keen to woo one of these cute critters themselves (ideally without a Snow White-level singsong).

Recent findings suggest that look, I'll level with you; I know that squirrels might not be everyone's favorite garden visitors. After all, they're notorious for raiding bird feeders, digging up freshly planted bulbs and burying nuts in flower pots. Before you declare war on these bushy-tailed garden acrobats, though, there's another side to consider... and not just the fact that they're the birth month animal for May babies everywhere.

Yes, squirrels can actually play a surprisingly useful role in the garden and wider ecosystem. From helping disperse tree seeds to spreading beneficial fungi, these busy little mammals contribute more to the natural world than you might realise. And they're also wonderfully entertaining to watch, with their energetic antics, impressive climbing skills and habit of darting between trees (so much so that it's well worth adding this charmingly rustic squirrel house to your backyard).

Industry observers note that it's easy to focus on the damage squirrels can sometimes cause, but they also provide several ecological benefits. By digging and burying seeds, for example, they can help newly introduced trees and plants establish themselves, not to mention turn over small patches of soil.

Squirrels eat mushrooms and other fungi, helping disperse fungal spores which go on to form crucial relationships with tree roots, helping trees access nutrients and water. And let's not forget, either, that they are – sorry – an important food source for predators such as hawks, owls, foxes and other wildlife.

Rather than trying to keep squirrels out of your yard, why not consider making them feel welcome? With the right food, shelter and a little patience, you can encourage them to visit regularly and gradually become more comfortable with your presence.

Here's how to befriend a squirrel, then, along with some top tips on what to feed them and how to enjoy their firm without sacrificing your bird feeders or flowers.

It has been revealed that squirrels are naturally drawn to gardens with plenty of trees, shrubs and places to hide. The easiest way to befriend a squirrel, then, is to offer up mature trees (which provide opportunities for climbing, nesting and foraging,) and dense shrubs that offer shelter from predators and bad weather.

In a recent development, oak, hickory, beech and walnut trees are particularly valuable to many North American squirrel species because they produce nuts and seeds that provide natural food. So, if you have space, consider planting native trees and shrubs that offer food and shelter throughout the year.

One of the easiest ways to make your yard appealing to squirrels is to let nature do some of the work. Rather than removing every fallen nut, seed head or piece of natural debris, then, consider leaving a few areas where wildlife can forage.

Trees that produce acorns, walnuts and hickory nuts can provide valuable food, while berry-producing native shrubs offer additional opportunities for wildlife to feed. And you could also leave some fallen leaves in quieter areas of the garden, as these support insects and other small creatures that contribute to the wider ecosystem.

Anyone who's ever managed to befriend a squirrel before will tell you, in no uncertain terms, that offering small quantities of food always goes a long way!

Recent findings suggest that unsalted hazelnuts, walnuts and pecans in their shells provides a natural foraging activity. Sunflower seeds, too, are a familiar food source for many squirrel species, although they should only be offered in modest quantities. And plain pumpkin seeds can provide another occasional treat, too.

Natural food from your garden should always be the first port of call, of course; acorns, tree seeds and other naturally available foods are preferable to making squirrels dependent on a regular supply from you (especially as healthy wild squirrels don't really need supplementary feeding).

On that note, remember not to overfeed; the trick here is to only offer a small amount, remove uneaten food and avoid creating a feeding station that attracts large numbers of animals or unwanted pests. And take care to keep any feeding equipment clean, too, as communal feeding areas can allow diseases to spread between squirrels.

Like other wildlife, squirrels need access to fresh water, and a shallow birdbath or a wildlife water dish like this one can provide a convenient drinking spot, particularly during hotter, drier weather.

In a recent development, just as you would for your beloved birds, make sure the water is kept clean and refreshed regularly. Adding a few stones can also provide a helpful foothold for smaller creatures, too, and don't forget to position the water somewhere squirrels can reach safely (ideally near trees or shrubs that offer a quick escape route).

Perhaps the most rewarding part of welcoming squirrels into your garden is watching them gradually become more comfortable with your presence. Start by simply observing them from a distance, and then try to spend a little time in the garden without making sudden movements or approaching them.

According to recent reports, if you provide a small amount of food, use the same designated feeding area and let squirrels discover it independently. Over time, they may become accustomed to seeing you in the garden and feel more comfortable foraging while you're nearby.

Sources indicate that even if you are attempting to befriend a squirrel, please don't attempt to chase, touch or hand-feed them. Even seemingly friendly squirrels can bite or scratch if they feel threatened, and encouraging wildlife to approach people can create problems for both animals and humans.

If you want to welcome squirrels without losing your bird feeders, consider using squirrel-resistant feeders, particularly models with weight-activated mechanisms that close feeding ports when a heavier animal climbs aboard.

You can also install a squirrel baffle on feeder poles to prevent squirrels from climbing up to reach the food. And don't forget to position feeders away from nearby trees, fences and other launching points wherever possible, as squirrels are surprisingly good at jumping.

If you'd like to provide food for both birds and squirrels, consider giving them separate feeding areas. This can help reduce competition, although it won't guarantee that squirrels won't investigate the bird feeders.

If you want to stop squirrels digging up your flower bulbs, be sure to protect the plants you want to keep safe. This might mean covering newly planted bulbs with wire mesh or use protective bulb baskets, as these allow plants to grow while making it much harder for squirrels to reach the bulbs.

Industry observers note that alternatively, you can also cover the soil in containers with suitable mesh or another physical barrier, particularly during the autumn planting season. This approach allows squirrels to continue visiting the garden while protecting the areas where their digging is less welcome.

Squirrels might occasionally test a gardener's patience, but they're also fascinating little creatures that play a role in supporting healthy ecosystems.

Recent findings suggest that if you want to befriend a squirrel, you may find that simply providing natural food sources, shelter and fresh water does the trick! And if you do decide to put out the occasional treat, remember that moderation and good hygiene are notable; these are wild animals, and the aim should be to encourage natural visits rather than turn them into pets.

According to recent reports, oh sure, you might not be able to stop every squirrel from investigating your bird feeders or digging in your flower beds, but learning to accommodate these lively visitors? Well, that could make your garden a much more interesting place to spend time in the long run...

Did You Know You Have a Birth Month Winter Bird? Here's All 12 and Their Special Meanings

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2162 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seasons are shifting, which means our feathered friends are about to embark upon a changing of the guard...
  • It's not a silly question, by any means.
  • Sources indicate that with that in mind, then, what if every month had its own winter bird to call its own?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seasons are shifting, which means our feathered friends are about to embark upon a changing of the guard... so which is your birth month winter bird, you ask?

It's not a silly question, by any means. After all, some birds migrate south for winter, some arrive from further north, and year-round residents shift their habits. And, from the brilliant red cardinal perched against a snowy backdrop to the tiny dark-eyed junco hopping beneath a bird feeder, these seasonal visitors have plenty of personality.

Sources indicate that with that in mind, then, what if every month had its own winter bird to call its own? What might it reveal about the people born under its wings?

Now, we’re already familiar with the idea of a classic birth month bird, not to mention the birth month owl and birth month bird of prey, but what might the unique traits that make each winter bird so wonderful say about our own personalities?

Some are bold and charismatic, others are quiet and contemplative, and a few are wonderfully independent. All, though, are beautiful in their own special way, and so much fun to watch as they go about their business over the colder months.

With that in mind, then, I've paired 12 fascinating winter birds with the personality traits commonly associated with each birth month, along with a few easy ways you can make your garden a more welcoming place for them. Time to grab yourself a motion-activated wildlife camera with night vision, like the GardePro on Amazon, then, and start reading...

And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

It has been revealed that if you're born in January, you're likely to be headstrong, disciplined and hardworking (all of which are, natural leadership qualities, just in case you fancied informing your boss). Naturally, then, your birth month winter bird is a wonderful reflection of that determination: the snow bunting.

These beautiful little birds are highly social during winter, often gathering in flocks to forage for seeds in open fields and along shorelines, while their ability to thrive in bitterly cold conditions is rather impressive for such a small bird.

Like January babies, basically, they don't shy away from a challenge; they meet it head-on! To help them do this, be sure to leave native grasses and seed-producing plants standing where possible, rather than tidying every corner of your garden.

In a recent development, one of the most iconic birds in the world, the striking snowy owl has brilliant white plumage, piercing yellow eyes and an unmistakable presence. They spend much of the year in the Arctic, but some travel south during winter, occasionally appearing in northern parts of the United States (although they tend to favour wide-open landscapes, including coastal dunes, fields and other exposed areas where they can hunt).

Often solitary hunters, February's birth month winter bird gets by on its own instincts and remarkable ability to spot prey from a distance. It's also wonderfully adapted to its harsh environment, making it a fitting symbol of independence, deep-thinking, and inner strength.

To help snowy owls out over the colder months, avoid using rodenticides that can poison birds of prey, turn your garden into an owl hangout (it only takes five plants), and always give any owl you encounter plenty of space.

March babies are often associated with introspection, creativity, compassion and a thoughtful nature. It makes a whole lot of sense, then, that their birth month winter bird is the dark-eyed junco, a small but charming visitor that brings plenty of life to colder gardens.

Sometimes nicknamed the snowbird, dark-eyed juncos tend to spend much of their time quietly hopping around on the ground, searching for fallen seeds beneath trees and feeders. As such, they're a lovely match for March personalities: observant, gentle and happy to enjoy the quieter things in life.

Recent findings suggest that if you fancy seeing more in your garden, remember that juncos are particularly fond of feeding on the ground, so provide a sheltered feeding area with small seeds. Leaving native grasses and seed heads standing also gives them more natural foraging opportunities.

Shop Junco Bird Feeding Essentials:.

If you're an April baby, you're thought to be charismatic, energetic, straightforward and naturally confident. As such, there's perhaps no better bird to represent you than the unmistakable blue jay.

With its brilliant blue plumage, distinctive crest and loud calls, the blue jay certainly knows how to make itself noticed. These intelligent members of the crow family have bold personalities that often make them one of the most entertaining birds to watch, in fact.

Industry observers note that blue jays are also clever problem-solvers, not to mention never afraid to make their presence known. Plant native oak trees and other nut-producing species to provide natural food and shelter to help them out, and remember that they also enjoy unsalted peanuts , so you can occasionally offer some in a suitable feeder.

I know, I know; a wild turkey might not feel like the most glamorous birth month winter bird, but hear me out! May personalities are often described as sociable, talented, loyal and strong-willed. And wild turkeys? Why, they're highly social, often gathering in flocks during winter as they search for food, not to mention putting on some impressive courtship displays.

According to recent reports, they're also resourceful foragers, searching through woodland floors for seeds, nuts, berries and insects. During colder months, they can be spotted scratching through leaf litter and searching beneath trees for whatever food they can find. To help yours out, then, take care to leave natural cover in place where possible, and avoid using pesticides that reduce the insects and other natural food sources they rely on.

Known for its melancholy-sounding coo, the gentle mourning dove is a familiar sight across much of the United States, often seen perched on telephone wires, fences and tree branches, or quietly searching the ground for seeds.

They're also known for their strong pair bonds, with partners often working together to raise their young, so it's easy to see why this bird suits June babies (especially as they tend to be such romantic dreamers). It's a birth month winter bird that perfectly aligns with all of that sensitivity and imagination.

According to recent reports, remember, mourning doves enjoy feeding on the ground, so provide a clean feeding area with something like sunflower hearts if you want to see them in your garden. Plant some native seed-producing plants and shrubs, too, to help provide natural food and shelter.

Recent findings suggest that july babies are adventurous free spirits known for their cheerful and (ahem) slightly slightly eccentric personalities, not to mention their strong protective streaks when it comes to family. It was inevitable, then, that the snow goose would prove their birth month winter bird.

Known for their impressive journeys between breeding and wintering grounds, snow geese are often spotted travelling in enormous flocks that fill the sky with their distinctive calls. They are also strongly connected to family life; young birds travel with their parents, and family groups can remain together during migration and winter.

If you want to help your feathery soulmate out, remember that snow geese depend on healthy wetlands, grasslands and agricultural landscapes during migration and winter. Supporting wetland conservation and protecting natural resting and feeding areas, then, is one of the best ways to keeo them thriving.

It makes so much sense that August babies get the delightful red-breasted nuthatch as their birth month winter bird, as it sums up all their best qualities perfectly. Yes, this little bird might be small, but it certainly doesn't lack confidence. One of its most entertaining habits is climbing headfirst down tree trunks, something it does with remarkable ease as it searches for insects and seeds hidden in the bark.

According to recent reports, during autumn and winter, red-breasted nuthatches also collect and store conifer seeds, helping ensure they have food available when conditions become more challenging. They're hardworking, resourceful and rather determined, making them a lovely match for August birthdays.

In a recent development, to help them out, try to plant native trees such as pine, spruce and fir where appropriate for your region. You can also offer sunflower seeds, peanuts or suet in a clean feeder, particularly during colder weather.

Intelligent, spiritual, organized and analytical, September babies tend to be more successful in life (genuinely; look it up!) and thus are represented by the pine siskin.

Recent findings suggest that these small finches might be easy to overlook at first, but they're fascinating little birds. They are adaptable, clever, and brimming with plenty of resourcefulness, though, which is why you often seen clinging to the tips of pine branches and even hanging upside down as they extract seeds from cones.

According to recent reports, sure, they're rather unpredictable visitors, as their movements depend heavily on food availability; this means that some gardens might welcome large flocks one winter and see very few the next. To keep them flocking, grow native conifers and other seed-producing plants to provide natural food, as well as nyjer (thistle) seed and sunflower hearts in finch feeders.

As an October baby myself, I'm more than happy to see this charming wanderer as my birth month winter bird! Especially as, with its striking yellow, black and white plumage and enormous pale bill, this chunky finch is one of North America's most distinctive birds.

Evening grosbeaks are adventurous travellers, sometimes moving considerable distances in search of food during autumn and winter. They're also wonderfully sociable, often gathering in groups around food sources and making quite an impression when they arrive at a backyard feeder.

For October birthdays, they're a lovely symbol of persistence, confidence and a little good fortune. After all, spotting one can feel like winning a small birdwatching lottery (although you can boost your chances with a handful of black-oil sunflower seeds, which can be offered in a sturdy platform feeder).

Empathetic, generous, brave and deeply determined, November-born souls are represented by one of North America's most magnificent waterbirds: the trumpeter swan.

According to recent reports, these enormous white swans are impressive in every sense, with long necks, powerful wings and a distinctive black bill. They are known for their strong pair bonds and devoted parenting, and their family groups can be particularly striking to see gliding across a winter lake. In fact, it's their loyalty, protective instincts and graceful strength that make them a beautiful match for November birthdays.

These aren't traditional garden birds, so you can help them by protecting local wetlands, ponds and freshwater habitats, and always taking care to avoid disturbing swans when they're resting or feeding.

Generous, patriotic, optimistic and willing to take a few risks? Yeah, obviously the birth month winter bird for December is the cardinal!

According to recent reports, known for their strong pair bonds and the way they communicate through a variety of musical calls, their cheerful appearance against bare branches and snowy gardens has led to them becoming something not unlike a symbol of hope during the festive season. In fact, many believe that if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st, you're owed 12 months of love, optimism, and luck for the year ahead.

If you want to help yours out, plant native berry-producing shrubs such as winterberry, serviceberry and dogwood to make your garden a one-stop destination for food, shelter, and nesting opportunities.

Whether you believe in the concept of a birth month winter bird or not, there's no denying that they serve as a lovely reminder of just how much wildlife is around us, even during the coldest months of the year.

It has been revealed that and perhaps the best part is that you don't have to wait for your own birth month to enjoy these feathered visitors. By planting native trees and shrubs, leaving seed heads standing, providing clean water and maintaining safe feeding areas, you can help make your garden a welcoming winter refuge for your feathered friends throughout the year.

Sources indicate that give it a go, I say! You'll do your bit for local wildlife and you might even discover a new favorite feathered friend along the way...

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Sources indicate that humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair. Many of us willingly put ourselves through torturous procedures to remove it from our legs, armpits, and just about anywhere else, while, at the same time, the quest to keep a full and lustrous head of hair fuels a billion-dollar hair growth industry. Since the 1980s, a chemical called Minoxidil has become increasingly popular as both a topical and oral treatment for baldness, but what few people realize is that the very product promising hair growth poses a serious risk to their pets. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) is warning consumers about minoxidil toxicity in cats and dogs, highlighting a danger that deserves considerably more attention.

According to recent reports, anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule. Cats rub against our heads, groom our hair, curl up on our pillows, and somehow manage to investigate just about everything we touch. These perfectly normal feline behaviors can turn deadly when minoxidil enters the picture.

The history of minoxidil shares similarities with another well-known human drug: Viagra, which essentially took a common side effect of the heart medication, sildenafil, and turned it into its primary purpose. In the 1970s, researchers developing a fresh blood pressure medication found that a common side effect of the drug, minoxidil, was hypertrichosis, aka excessive hair growth. Like the story of sildenafil, the makers of minoxidil leaned into this side effect, repurposing the drug as a treatment for hair loss.1.

In 1988, the FDA officially approved minoxidil, and it promptly gained popularity in products like Rogaine. Minoxidil works by widening blood vessels, a process called vasodilation, and altering the hair growth cycle to stimulate hair growth. But what helps us fight hair loss can be dangerous for our feline roommates.

A 2021 study published in the Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association examined 211 reported cases of topical minoxidil exposure in dogs and cats. Of the 87 animals that developed signs of poisoning, 62 were cats, and 25 were dogs. Eight cats died. A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology identified another 94 reported cases, including 68 cats, ten of which died. Notably, 55 of 57 cases involving accidental exposure to a person's minoxidil treatment involved cats.

It has been revealed that how does this happen? Topical minoxidil is applied directly to the scalp, either as a liquid using a dropper or as a foam spread with the fingers. Medication can remain on the hands, hair, or nearby surfaces. Cats don't need to break into the medicine cabinet; a little grooming, an affectionate head rub, or a snooze on a contaminated pillow may be enough to expose them. Some were even exposed through everyday contact with their follicle-challenged cat parents.

Minoxidil works by relaxing blood vessels and improving blood flow. In cats, however, the effects can become dangerously disruptive.

When absorbed, it can cause blood pressure to drop dramatically, a condition called hypotension. To compensate, the heart beats faster, but this doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Serious complications can follow, including fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema) or in the space surrounding them (pleural effusion). Breathing becomes increasingly difficult, and severe poisoning can progress to cardiovascular and respiratory failure.

Now, what should you look out for? You might notice unusual tiredness, weakness, vomiting, or a sudden loss of appetite. More concerningly, your kitty may start breathing faster than usual or appear to struggle for air. And here's the tricky part: some cats may initially seem perfectly fine.

It has been revealed that that's why a suspected exposure should never be brushed off simply because your cat appears normal. Waiting for visible signs of poisoning can waste valuable time.

Now that we are beginning to appreciate the risks this product poses to our pets, we have to wonder how many unexplained cat and dog deaths could be attributed to unknown minoxidil exposure.

Rapunzel may have had a tower to keep her hair safe, but cat owners need a different strategy: keeping minoxidil well away from curious paws.

If you use topical minoxidil, make sure you apply it in a room your cat cannot access. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water immediately afterward, and clean up any spills promptly. Used tissues, cotton pads, applicators, and empty containers should go straight into a secure bin. That tissue you casually leave on the bathroom counter? To your cat, it might look like just another interesting thing to investigate.

Industry observers note that and what about bedtime? If you apply minoxidil in your bedroom, make closing the door part of your nighttime routine. Your cat may protest being left out of the bedroom, especially if your pillow is their favorite sleeping spot, but keeping them away from treated hair, skin, pillows, and bedding can help prevent accidental contact with medication residue. Remember, allowing the product to dry does not guarantee that every surface is free from contamination.

Recent findings suggest that you might be wondering whether switching to oral minoxidil would solve the problem. Unfortunately, not entirely. Oral minoxidil is also toxic to cats if they accidentally ingest a tablet. Whichever formulation you use, keep the medication securely stored and well out of paws' reach. Or better yet, look into options that donât put your pet at risk.

Recent findings suggest that discuss your household's furry residents with the prescribing dermatologist and establish a routine that prevents accidental exposure. Cats are wonderfully persistent creatures. They may not appreciate a closed door or understand why their favorite pillow is suddenly off-limits, but a little inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping them safe.

If your cat licks minoxidil, contacts a spill, or may have groomed contaminated fur, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control service immediately, even if your kitty seems perfectly fine.

Recent findings suggest that treatment depends on the exposure and your cat's condition. It may involve hospitalization, cardiovascular monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous support, and medications to manage complications such as low blood pressure or fluid accumulation.

It has been revealed that never attempt to induce vomiting or administer home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinary professional. If medication is still on your cat's coat or skin, ask your veterinarian how to handle decontamination safely rather than delaying emergency care.

Unfortunately, not every cat survives minoxidil poisoning, making every accidental exposure a veterinary emergency.

It has been revealed that hair loss can affect confidence, and wanting to treat it is perfectly understandable. Minoxidil can be a valuable treatment for people experiencing certain types of hair loss, but sharing a home with a cat adds an crucial responsibility.

It has been revealed that preventing accidental poisoning starts with awareness. As pet parents, we need to be mindful of the products we bring into our homes, even those that seem perfectly harmless to us. From seemingly innocent houseplants and everyday foods to cleaning products, medications, and personal care treatments, many things we use routinely can pose risks to our feline companions. Before introducing something new into your home, take a moment to consider whether it is safe for your cat. A little research and a few precautions can make a world of difference.

Industry observers note that cats will continue doing what cats do best: following their humans, investigating everything, claiming the pillows, and showing affection on their own terms. We cannot expect them to understand why a particular patch of skin or a freshly treated pillow is suddenly off-limits. That responsibility belongs to us.

Sources indicate that thinning hair can be frustrating, even damaging to self-esteem, but itâs not a life-threatening condition. Losing a beloved pet to an avoidable medication exposure is a tragedy no one should have to experience.

Better bald than catless. Every single time.

Every Japanese Maple Needs Some TLC Before Winter – 6 Easy Tasks to Protect Your Prized Tree

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage.
  • Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as I write this, I cannot stop glancing at my Japanese maple, its entire canopy ablaze with crimson and orange foliage. It's my little jewel of the garden, a sentiment shared by many of my friends with these small trees in their landscapes.

Japanese maples (Acer palmatum) are counted among the most beautiful ornamental trees around, with their elegant branching structure, graceful canopy, and spectacular fall foliage. Since these trees are usually hardy down to USDA zone 4 or 5, they may shrug off winter cold. But that doesn’t make them immune to winter damage from the cold weather, harsh winds, and fluctuating soil moisture. Young trees and container trees are especially vulnerable.

Industry observers note that so you should have more than a few items on your list for Japanese maple tree care before winter. If not, you’ve come to the right place. This guide explains the six simple but essential tasks to ensure your Japanese maple makes it through winter with flying colors. You can do them at the same time as your other garden winterizing tasks.

According to recent reports, don’t worry too much about watering your Japanese maple during winter. When the leaves fall and the tree enters dormancy, it needs very little water. Water trees only if there has been no precipitation for several weeks and the ground is bone dry.

However, to help them through the winter, give them one final irrigation before the ground freezes. If the summer has been hot and/or dry, make this a deep watering. A soaker hose is ideal for delivering a slow, even soaking across the tree's root zone without wasting water. The Gilmour Round Soaker Hose from Amazon is a good option, as it distributes water evenly along its length.

Sources indicate that tuck a cozy blanket of mulch around your precious tree in November. Use something organic – wood chips or bark work well. Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot is a good option, made from natural, shredded wood. Layer up to 4 inches (10 cm) of mulch over the root zone. This protects the roots, holds heat in the soil, and prevents frost heaving.

Industry observers note that don’t make the mistake of piling the mulch up against the trunk in a “volcano” arrangement. The mulch should never touch the trunk since that can cause wood rot.

Industry observers note that is your Japanese maple a young tree you planted within the last three years? You’ll want to give the juvenile tree extra protection. This will also be true if you live in a region with an exceptionally cold winter.

In these circumstances, help your tree survive with insulation. Wrap vulnerable trunks or branches with burlap, such as this Riare Natural Burlap Plant Protection Wrap from Amazon, to shield them against harsh, drying winter winds. Leave the burlap loose enough to allow the tree to breathe.

According to recent reports, if your tree has broken or diseased branches, the best time to take those off is now, whenever you notice. And you should check regularly to spot problems early. But aside from this type of damage, do not give your Japanese maple a haircut in November or at any other point during dormancy. Pruning at this time can leave cuts vulnerable to disease and frost damage.

Industry observers note that would you have an energy drink just before bedtime? Of course not. And for all the same reasons, do not fertilize your Japanese maple in November. Fertilizer, especially nitrogen fertilizer, induces new growth just as the tree should be entering winter dormancy. This new growth is tender and will easily freeze in the first flush of winter weather, leading to dieback or split bark.

In spring, if your tree needs feeding, use a gentle, slow-release fertilizer, such as Espoma Organic Tree-tone (6-3-2) from Amazon. Apply sparingly, following the package instructions, as Japanese maples generally don't need much fertilizer.

It won’t surprise you to hear that container maple trees require more protection than a Japanese maple with its roots deep in the garden soil. Their roots are much closer to the cold air on all sides, and therefore can freeze or dry out faster.

You’ll want to take steps to protect a potted Japanese maple. A good first step is to insulate the containers with bubble wrap or burlap. Wrap the pots well and cluster the containers together near the house to attract radiant heat. It also helps to use pot feet, like Bosmere's Pot Toes, or even wood blocks to raise the containers off the cold ground and support good drainage.

In the most severe winters, you can move your container trees into a shelter, like an unheated garage or a sheltered porch.

Does your tree still have leaves as Thanksgiving arrives? This is normal, not a cause for alarm.

Trees have an abscission layer at the base of their leaf stems that releases the leaves to fall in the cold. But Japanese maples build this layer more slowly than other deciduous trees like red or sugar maples. And if you’ve had a mild autumn, this can delay leaf drop even further, even into December.

This means additional watering work for you. While your maple still has leaves, you’ll need to keep watering whenever the soil is dry. At the same time, rake up leaves that do fall and remove them. You don’t want soggy or decaying piles of maple leaves since this can encourage the spread of fungal spores.

According to recent reports, cats are famously persistent beggars, and a holiday table full of tempting smells gives them plenty of motivation. Although there are a handful of Thanksgiving dishes that are fine in small amounts, several can make a cat seriously ill, so it pays to know which is which before anything gets shared.

Industry observers note that the following foods are generally harmless for cats, provided the portions stay small and there are no pre-existing health complications. Of course, safe doesnât always mean healthy, and moderation is key. Just like people, cats also differ in what they like, and many will show no interest in some of these at all.

Plain turkey is the best choice, since cats are obligate carnivores and tend to love it. It needs to be free of skin, fat, bones, gravy, and spices, and a small piece is plenty. The best thing to do is set aside a small amount to cook without all the frills, rather than cleaning it later.

It has been revealed that plain, cooked pumpkin is non-toxic and good for a catâs digestion, and it may even soothe an upset stomach. A puree or mash works well. Pumpkin pie is a different matter, because the sugar and possible dairy arenât good for cats.

Apples are safe and offer vitamins C and K, calcium, and fiber. The seeds, leaves, and stems contain cyanide and must be removed, and the fruit should be chopped into small cubes.

Plain green beans, minus butter, spices, herbs, onion, or garlic, are a good source of fiber and can even stand in for regular treats. Broccoli is also safe if it is unseasoned and boiled or steamed. Itâs unlikely a cat will want it, but it provides antioxidants and supports digestion. As with any fresh food, itâs best to introduce it carefully. Cranberry sauce isnât toxic, but its sugar content makes it unhealthy, so only an incredibly small taste is appropriate.

Some Thanksgiving staples should never be shared, because they can make a cat quite ill.

Garlic, onions, leeks, scallions, and similar vegetables can be deadly even in small amounts, and garlic powder is particularly problematic. They damage a catâs red blood cells and lead to anemia, with signs such as weakness, a high heart rate, diarrhea, vomiting, and collapse. Cats are more sensitive to them than dogs, and symptoms have reportedly appeared after less than a teaspoon of cooked onion.

Many stuffings contain onions or garlic. Even without them, stuffing is usually rich with ingredients like turkey grease that can upset a catâs stomach. It wonât be deadly without those ingredients, but it has no nutritional value and can wreak havoc on digestion.

According to recent reports, bones should stay well out of reach. Cooked bones in particular can splinter or crack and could tear the mouth, break teeth, cause choking, or block the digestive system, and bacteria are a concern too. Keep them well out of reach.

Industry observers note that chocolate is incredibly toxic to cats, and the darker it is, the worse it gets. The theobromine and caffeine it contains can cause vomiting, muscle tremors, diarrhea, an abnormal heart rate, and seizures, and it can even lead to death. Anything else with caffeine, including coffee, is off limits as well.

Sources indicate that grapes and raisins can lead to kidney failure, and even a tiny amount of either, or related dried fruits like craisins, can cause illness. Signs include continuous vomiting, stomach distress, and hyperactivity. Some cats show no symptoms after eating them, but that isnât a reason to take the chance.

Gravy isnât toxic, but it is salty and fatty, which cats donât need much of. Those levels could cause further problems for a cat with heart trouble. A sneaky lick is nothing to worry about, but gravy shouldnât be mixed into a catâs food.

Industry observers note that A bowl of milk may seem harmless, but many cats are lactose intolerant. Dairy can give them a stomach ache, gas, or diarrhea, so itâs better to offer something from the safe list instead if theyâre sniffing around the kitchen.

Sources indicate that raw meat and fish can carry pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella that make cats ill, so avoid the temptation to drop some scraps as youâre preparing meals.

Sources indicate that A cat can share in the holiday with a nibble of plain turkey or a spoonful of pumpkin, but a few ordinary ingredients you may have around the table can cause illness and even death. With a little care over what goes into the bowl, both cat and family can enjoy a safe and happy Thanksgiving.

This Easy Lasagna Gardening Hack Transforms Tired Soil Over Winter – No Digging Required

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task.
  • According to recent reports, so just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening.
  • Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that just because you like gardening doesn’t mean that you enjoy every landscape task. Some of us gardeners love planting flowers but don’t enjoy raking leaves. Others like tucking mulch around their shrubs but won’t pull weeds. But digging up the garden dirt and turning it over is not high on anyone’s list of favorite tasks.

According to recent reports, so just say no to digging in the fall and say yes to lasagna gardening. It’s a clever, no-dig technique that works best in fall. Leave the shovel in the garage and instead, stack layers of cardboard, fallen leaves, and other organic materials over the garden soil, letting them break down naturally over winter. The result is fertile planting beds for spring.

Ready to get “cooking”? Here, I will walk you through the four-layer lasagna garden recipe.

It has been revealed that of course you love your garden, but wouldn’t it be nice if the garden could do most of the work of preparing the beds for spring planting? Lasagna gardening, aka no-dig or no-till gardening, allows your garden to do most of the work of decomposition and replenishment. The technique is really cold composting in place.

Sources indicate that this low-effort process works like home composting: alternate layers of green and brown materials, then let them break down into the soil. Cut grass and kitchen scraps are green materials; cardboard and dried leaves are brown materials. Your “lasagna” is a compost heap waiting to happen.

In a recent development, you can also think of lasagna gardening as mimicking the forest floor. It works the same way soil is built up in a woodland. First, leaves pile up and decompose on the forest floor. Along come microbes and worms that transform that debris into rich soil. Lasagna gardening follows the same pattern, making your garden bed into a soil ecosystem.

According to recent reports, when you make a lasagna for dinner, you just layer up the pasta, the ragù, the sauce, and grated cheese, then pop it in the oven. Without any additional work on your part, a luscious dinner will be ready when it is time to eat.

A winter lasagna garden uses the same system. You stack up four layers, then leave it to decompose. Without any additional work on your part, your garden will have rich, fertile soil for spring. Here are the four key layers.

According to recent reports, think of cardboard as the weed barrier. First, weed-whack or mow the area to cut down any weeds or grass. A cordless string trimmer, like this Worx model, makes things easier.

Then, lay sheets of flattened cardboard right over the soil in your garden, using overlapping layers to cover the entire area. Heavy, corrugated cardboard works best to keep grass and weeds out while still welcoming earthworms. After that is done, douse all of the cardboard with lukewarm water.

According to recent reports, this is the carbon layer, supporting soil microbes and providing structural aeration. I like using dry autumn leaves (what else are you going to do with them?), but a thick layer of any type of brown material will work, giving your garden soil a carbon-rich environment. Alternatives include straw, peat moss, sawdust, wood chips, or shredded newspaper.

If you don't have enough waste materials to hand, a bag of garden straw mulch, like this HealthiStraw GardenStraw from Walmart, is an easy way to bulk up this layer.

Here’s the “compost” element of the lasagna. Your green materials will be in charge of making the garden soil a nitrogen-rich environment that heats up and fuels the decay process. Together with the brown material, they make the garden one giant compost pile. You can use kitchen waste, but also toss in some grass clippings, coffee grounds, or even manure.

If you can't source enough green material for free, then pick up a bag of composted cow manure, such as Black Kow, available at Home Depot.

According to recent reports, you aren’t limited to one layer of brown material and one layer of green. Keep right on stacking alternating layers, using about twice as much brown as green. Two, three, or even four alternating layers of organic material can speed things up for your garden bed.

Flattened cardboard lays the foundation for the lasagna; compost or topsoil serves as a top cap. For a ready-made option, try Back to the Roots Organic Compost from Home Depot. This is especially vital if you are planning on planting immediately. This rich layer is at the top of the pile so that your seeds will have what it takes to establish strong roots in short order.

A lasagna garden is an attractive option if low-maintenance is a priority. Once you create your lasagna, wonderful things begin to happen and keep on happening all winter. The green and brown layered materials function as a compost pile, and the constant interplay between them heats up, then breaks down the entire pile, enriching the soil.

Industry observers note that the bottom layer of cardboard in the garden lasagna blocks weeds from invading the latest, appealing soil. What had been a used-up garden transforms into a sanctuary for your plants, with loose, fertile soil. This makes the next growing season easy and exciting.

Sources indicate that if you “build” a lasagna garden in the late autumn or early winter, the magic starts right away. The four layers do their job: the cardboard prevents weed growth, the brown and green layers do their compost dance and decompose into the soil, and the top layer is ready to welcome seeds.

This lasagna garden should be fully decomposed and ready to plant by the following April or May. Autumn rain and winter moisture keep the layers moist. The organic layers require at least several months to break down.

According to recent reports, if you put in a lasagna garden in spring or summer, you do so with the thought of immediate planting. Just dig small pockets into the top layer of the bed.
